items.summary: Tanner Kohler of Nielsen Norman Group reviewed new AI-first development playbooks from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI. He says they use UX only as background input for the AI, and skip user research and testing with real people. He asks UX teams to own the design-system context, add user-value checks before work starts, and track signals like task abandonment after launch.
items.title: NN/g: AI-native software processes treat UX as just context for code generation
items.why: This is a ready-made argument Narek can use at Ameriabank when AI speeds up delivery. It shows how a designer can keep a seat at the table: own the context files, the research and the quality bar.

items.summary: Raluca Budiu argues that UX now has two kinds of users: people, and AI agents that act for people. She suggests the name 'experience design' for a field that covers both, plus the handoffs between human and agent. The goal does not change: help people reach their goals.
items.title: NN/g proposes 'experience design' as UX expands to cover AI agents
items.why: This gives Narek simple language for a new type of design work. Showing that he designs for both humans and agents could make his portfolio stand out.

items.summary: Affinity now has one iPad app that covers vector, photo and layout work, with a touch-first interface. It is free with a Canva account, while AI features need a paid plan. It supports Apple Pencil pressure and tilt, and it uses the same .af file format as the desktop app.
items.title: Canva launches a free all-in-one Affinity app for iPad
items.why: It is a free, professional tool for sketching and illustration on the go. Narek could use it for MyAmeria Star artwork without paying for Adobe.

items.summary: Creative Bloq looks at a loud lettering style: rough brush strokes with an upward slant. It now appears on many AI-made posters in cafes and village halls. It is not a real typeface. AI image tools copy it from old posters and ads. The writer says it now looks clearly artificial.
items.title: The 'AI brush font' look is now called the new Comic Sans
items.why: Generic AI styles quickly make brands look cheap. When Narek uses AI for visuals, he should set strict type and art direction rules, so the work still feels like Ameriabank.

items.summary: ChatGPT can now turn a prompt or a photo into an animated GIF. You can change its speed and edit single frames. You can also save reference images, such as a character, and reuse them later. In the API there are two new models: a fast one called Flare and a more detailed one called Sunburst. Through the API, the model can also produce an editable SVG (vector) file.
items.title: OpenAI launches Images 2.6: GIFs in ChatGPT, saved references and SVG output in the API
items.why: Fast GIFs and vector output make it cheap to test illustrations, empty states and small animations, for example for a kids' app like MyAmeria Star. Saved references help keep one mascot looking the same across many screens.

items.summary: About 22% of Canva's staff will lose their jobs, change roles or be asked to move. CEO Melanie Perkins said growth slowed for the first time in ten years. Canva will merge three groups into one product organisation, fold narrow specialist roles into broader ones and remove management layers. Perkins wants Canva to 'refound' itself around small teams that make their own decisions.
items.title: Canva cuts or relocates 1,271 roles and merges Product, Growth and Platform teams
items.why: A top design-tool company now prefers broad, hands-on people in small teams over narrow specialists. To stay valuable in the UK market, Narek can show range: research, systems, prototyping in code and business impact.

items.summary: Figma's revenue grew 43% to $391.4M in the third quarter. By 31 October, 65% of customers paying over $10,000 a year used the Figma agent every week. Its MCP server, which lets AI coding tools read and write Figma files, grew fastest of all its products. Code Layers, which put working code onto the canvas, is now in open beta.
items.title: Figma Q3: 65% of large customers use its agent weekly; MCP usage triples
items.why: This shows where the job is going: designers who connect Figma, design systems and code agents. Narek's design-system work at Ameriabank is a good place to try the MCP and Code Layers workflow.

items.summary: Revolut's value rose 53% in a year, through a sale of existing shares to big investors. It now has more than 80 million retail customers in over 40 countries. It has conditional approval for a US national bank and plans to launch it in the first half of 2027. It already runs banks in the UK, Mexico, Australia and New Zealand.
items.title: Revolut valued at $115B in share sale as it prepares a US bank for 2027
items.why: Revolut is the benchmark for super-app banking UX and a major UK design employer. Its growth means more product design roles in London, and its patterns shape what customers expect from MyAmeria.

items.summary: Uncommon's new outdoor campaign for British Airways uses dark, moody photos of puddles in the rain. Each puddle reflects a plane, and the line reads 'It's Always Sunny Somewhere' with a warm destination. Daniel Benson shot it in an unscripted, documentary style. The posters are running in London.
items.title: British Airways 'Puddles' posters by Uncommon show sunny places in rain reflections
items.why: This is a clear lesson in art direction: one simple idea, a real photo and a short line. It is a good model for bank campaigns that need emotion without clichés.

items.summary: Cat Wu led product for Claude Code and Cowork at Anthropic. She is joining OpenAI to lead product management for Core Products, the group behind ChatGPT, the API and Codex. She says her focus will be reliable agents. She is the third Claude Code team member to leave in about two weeks.
items.title: Claude Code's product lead Cat Wu moves from Anthropic to OpenAI
items.why: Narek is starting to ship code with AI agents. The race between Claude Code and Codex is heating up, so expect fast changes in both tools. It is smart not to lock workflows into only one of them.

items.summary: Reviews of Apple's first touchscreen Mac, with an OLED 'PROLED XDR' display, arrived as it reached buyers. Touch supports swipe, pinch-to-zoom, drag-and-drop and double-tap. Some controls, like the window buttons, grow when your finger is close. Reviewers say touch is nice to have, but the trackpad is still better for precise work.
items.title: First touchscreen MacBook Pro reviews: macOS adapts to fingers
items.why: Web and desktop banking screens may now be used by touch on Macs too. Hit areas, hover states and gestures need a fresh check in design-system components.

items.summary: Epic Games made its whole Quixel Megascans library free on the Fab marketplace. It has about 23,000 scanned 3D models, surfaces and plants. The licence lets you use the assets in any engine or tool. New terms also allow using them to train AI models.
items.title: Epic makes its 23,000-asset Megascans 3D library free, AI training allowed
items.why: Free, high-quality 3D assets make it easier to try 3D in UI, such as onboarding scenes or reward moments in a kids' banking app, without a big budget.

items.summary: Anthropic launched two versions of the same new model on 9 November. Fable 5.2 is open to everyone, and Mythos 5.2 (with fewer cybersecurity and biology limits) goes only to vetted organisations. Both are faster than the 5.1 versions, and API prices dropped to $8/$40 per million input/output tokens.
items.title: Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
items.why: This is the model family behind the Claude tools you use every day. Faster, cheaper models make large design-automation jobs more affordable.

items.summary: Google showed two eighth-generation AI chips on 9 November: one for confidential inference and one for very long context windows.
items.title: Google unveils TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max chips
items.why: Long-context chips make it cheaper to feed whole design systems and codebases to AI, which matters for your automation plans.

items.summary: The London studio redesigned the identity of the famous Colorplan paper range, drawing on Plan 8, its 1960s predecessor. In the same week Transform featured Butterfly Cannon's 'Bad Appel' Calvados identity.
items.title: Bibliothèque gives GF Smith's Colorplan paper a new global identity
items.why: A good example of using a brand's own history as the creative idea, an art-direction skill you can apply to Star.

items.summary: Smashing's 10 November newsletter, sent to over 170,000 readers, announced December workshops by Vitaly Friedman, including UX Strategy and How to Measure UX and Design Impact.
items.title: Smashing announces December workshops on UX strategy and measuring design impact
items.why: Measuring design impact is the skill that turns your Star work into portfolio numbers.

items.summary: United now stops personal AI agents from booking on its systems, citing privacy and regulatory concerns. It is one of the first big consumer brands to openly refuse agent traffic.
items.title: United Airlines blocks personal AI assistants from booking flights
items.why: Companies are deciding whether AI agents may act for customers. Banks face the same choice, so it's a design question for you.

items.summary: Starling's 'talk to transact' feature lets customers type or say a payment request to the in-app assistant. The assistant prepares the payment and the customer approves it with one tap. It rolls out to all retail customers by the end of 2026, alongside a new AI 'smart tool' every week.
items.title: Starling Bank lets customers send money by talking to the app
items.why: A real UK bank shipping agentic payments with a human approval step: exactly the trust pattern a MyAmeria AI assistant would need. Study the flow.

items.summary: Fortune reported, and OpenAI confirmed, that robotics researchers now sit in the main research team and hardware staff moved to the Applied group. OpenAI's bet is that general models like GPT-6 Astra can control robots without a separate specialist team.
items.title: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team
items.why: It shows how fast general models are taking over specialist work, the same shift that is changing design roles.

items.summary: OpenAI launched a beta hub where companies can claim and verify their presence in ChatGPT, see visibility metrics and set up brand agents. Ad buyers are already questioning part of their Google search budgets.
items.title: ChatGPT opens business profiles and brand agents
items.why: Brands, including banks, will soon design how they appear inside AI assistants, not only on their own apps and websites.

items.summary: The popular open-source tool for running AI models locally released a stable 1.0 with semantic versioning and support for more than 150 model architectures.
items.title: llama.cpp reaches version 1.0
items.why: Running models on your own laptop is getting easier, which helps with private prototypes and offline AI features.

items.summary: HNTrends found AI mentioned in 51.6% of November's 'Who is Hiring?' posts, up from 30% two years ago. Total postings in 2026 are at their lowest yearly average since 2013.
items.title: Over half of Hacker News job posts now mention AI
items.why: Fewer jobs, and more of them asking for AI. Make AI fluency visible in your CV and portfolio before you apply abroad.

items.summary: Since Nov 13, US Pro users can let ChatGPT buy things with a Visa, Mastercard or Amex card. You approve each purchase with Face ID, and the card network issues a token tied to that exact merchant, item list and total, so the shop never sees your card number. Simon Taylor likes that rewards and dispute rights stay with the card, but notes that dispute rules are not public yet and a biometric check for every purchase may get tiring.
items.title: ChatGPT Wallet: OpenAI starts letting its agent pay with your real card
items.why: This is the trust-and-confirmation pattern for agent payments, built in production. If MyAmeria ever adds an AI assistant that can move money, you'll need the same pieces: clear approval, tight limits, and a way to dispute.

items.summary: Nielsen reviews AutoAnalysis, a living meta-analysis from Harvard and MIT researchers that updates itself every month. Where AI and humans competed directly, AI won 68% of the time. Human–AI teams beat both solo performers in only 32% of cases, and in creative work such as design the gain from teaming has turned negative. The same roundup has a practical guide: use a toggle group (segmented control) instead of a dropdown when there are 2–5 options.
items.title: Jakob Nielsen: in 420 studies, human + AI teams lose to the best solo performer
items.why: This challenges the 'human in the loop' idea behind much of your AI workflow. Find the steps where you add value and let AI work alone on the rest. The toggle-group rule is something you can check in MyAmeria today.

items.summary: Since 1 July 2026, product, UX/UI, digital and graphic designers have had their own endorsement route, so they no longer have to squeeze into arts and culture. Lawyers note that a UX designer whose recognition comes mainly through a tech product may still fit better under the Digital Technology route.
items.title: The UK Global Talent visa now has a dedicated Design Industry pathway
items.why: This is the most direct route to your UK goal. Start an evidence folder now: published case studies, talks, awards, press mentions and letters from peers.

items.summary: In a Nov 12 filing, Nvidia said Huang is leaving as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress is acting CEO while the board searches for a permanent one, and Harvey Jones becomes the board's first chair. This came days after a board investigation into Huang's personal conduct began.
items.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO; CFO Colette Kress steps in as interim
items.why: Nvidia makes most of the chips behind the AI tools you use. A leadership gap there could change how quickly those tools improve and what they cost through 2027.

items.summary: Bloomberg reports that orders for the shares already far exceed supply, about 7 times over by one count. Pricing is planned for Wednesday, Nov 18, with trading on Nasdaq from the next day, which could make it one of the largest IPOs ever.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO is reportedly several times oversubscribed ahead of Nov 18 pricing
items.why: Claude is a core part of how you work. A public Anthropic will face pressure on pricing and enterprise features, so expect product news to come faster.

items.source: Lenny's Newsletter / How I AI (via newsletter)
items.summary: On How I AI, Claire Vo ran Fable 5.2 on real jobs: a branded animated video, furniture assembly steps from blurry photos, a code migration plan, and a 3D typewriter. It was fast, worked on its own, and made the best animation she has seen from a model. Its own visual design was unattractive, though it followed a brand system well when it was given one, so she still uses Opus 5.5 as her default.
items.title: Claire Vo tests Claude Fable 5.2: great at animation and agents, weak at taste
items.why: This shows how to split work between models. Give Fable your design system and motion tasks, but don't let it make visual decisions without strong direction.

items.summary: Brad Frost argues that AI hype is not the same as best practice. Teams frustrated by inconsistent AI output are turning back to design systems, because tokens, component structure and governance are what make AI output consistent. The post also links free sample lessons from his AI & Design Systems course.
items.title: Brad Frost: design-system foundations matter more in the AI era, not less
items.why: This supports your plan to teach AI the MyAmeria design system. The sample lessons on tokens and AI are a quick way to check your approach against his.

items.summary: The latest Smashing newsletter points to AI UX Playground, a library of more than 150 patterns, demos and teardowns for streaming, agent-based and tool-using interfaces. Vitaly Friedman's 'Design Patterns for AI Interfaces' workshop runs Nov 16–24.
items.title: Smashing: 150+ AI interface patterns, plus Vitaly Friedman's AI-UX workshop this week
items.why: AI interface patterns are among the most requested skills in senior design job posts, and studying them gives you material for case studies.

items.summary: This UX Collective essay argues that AI is merging roles back together, so leaders who still design hands-on are in demand again. It cites Figma's State of the Designer 2026, where most designers still define craft as visual polish rather than problem solving.
items.title: Smaller teams want design leaders who still make things
items.why: This describes your profile: you build systems and products yourself with AI. It's a useful way to position yourself for Design Lead roles abroad.

items.summary: Designers who started at agencies and those who started in-house reach management at about the same rate. But in this sample, the in-house starters became VP about 4.8 times as often.
items.title: Survey of 119 design leaders: in-house starters reach VP far more often
items.why: Your career has been in-house product work, which this data suggests is the stronger path to senior leadership.

items.summary: Your LinkedIn job alerts this week were mostly US roles. The EU exception is pasiona in Barcelona, which is hiring a senior designer for generative-AI and enterprise products and is marked as actively hiring.
items.title: Open role: Senior UX/UI & Product Designer (GenAI & enterprise) at pasiona, Barcelona
items.why: It matches your AI-product focus and would be a European step toward the UK. Read the post to check language and relocation requirements before you apply.

items.summary: Cat How, president of D&AD's 2026 New Brand Identity jury and founder of How&How, explains three ways branding has changed. She argues that as AI makes production cheap, judgment and taste matter more.
items.title: D&AD: why taste is becoming the rarest commodity in branding
items.why: Art direction is taste you can defend. This gives you language to explain your creative decisions, for example the Star claymation style.

items.summary: Creative Bloq looks at AI products, including Ideogram, Elva and Clusia, that hired respected studios for their identities instead of generating them. It asks what this says about trust and standing out.
items.title: Why AI companies keep hiring human studios for their branding
items.why: It shows that human art direction still defines the premium tier. That's useful context when you present visual work to stakeholders.

items.summary: Alibaba's new flagship model is a 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with a 1-million-token context window. Its weights are not public. Alibaba says it leads rivals on coding benchmarks and that it filtered the training data to reduce cyberattack risk. Artificial Analysis scores it 43 on its Intelligence Index, above the previous Qwen model.
items.title: Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max and says it cuts task costs by 60%
items.why: Cheaper strong models make it more affordable to run the design-automation agents you are building.

items.summary: The Wall Street Journal reports that the Trump administration plans to give a group of US AI companies an official 'national champion' status. The list includes Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic.
items.title: US government plans to name Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic and others 'AI national champions'
items.why: Government backing could shape which AI tools reach banks and other regulated companies outside the US, including in Armenia.

body: ## What happened

Optimizely Web is a tool for experiments. A company adds one small script from Optimizely's servers, and that script changes the page for different visitors. Each project also has a field for custom code. On 16 November, someone wrote a loader into that field for many customers. The file still came from Optimizely's real domain, with a valid certificate. So browsers and security rules trusted it. The sites themselves were never hacked.

The first infected snippet appeared at 04:21 UTC, on the BBC. During the day the attacker rebuilt the payload 26 times, always adding features. A card skimmer was added at 13:43. Most sites were cleaned between about 20:40 and 21:10. Report URI confirmed that all files were clean at 23:11.
## What the code did

It looked for real crypto wallet addresses in text, forms, links and the clipboard, and replaced them with the attacker's addresses. It read card number, expiry date and CVV from forms and sent them to the attacker's server. Cards typed into hosted payment iframes (payment fields served by a separate provider) were safe. On iPhones and iPads it chose an exploit kit based on the iOS version. Older devices reloaded the page every 60 seconds.

Public blockchain data shows about $7,000 in stolen crypto. Nobody knows yet how many cards or cookies were taken. Optimizely has not explained how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customers.
## Why defences failed

A Content Security Policy (CSP) is a header that tells the browser which scripts may run and where data may be sent. Report URI tested the victims' policies. 68 organisations had no CSP at all. Allowing Optimizely's domain did not help, because the bad code came from that domain. The setting 'unsafe-eval' let a hidden backup copy run at HSBC. A strict connect-src rule stopped card and cookie theft, but not address swapping inside the page.

Report URI advises Optimizely users to search their custom code for the attacker's domain and for 'atob(', check who has write access, and change passwords and tokens. Card data typed on 16 November should be treated as exposed. Visitors should update to iOS 18.7.3 or 26.3 or later and check their card statements.
points: On 16 November 2026, an attacker put malicious code inside Optimizely Web snippets. These are scripts that brands load on every page to run A/B tests.
Report URI checked 1,611 snippets and found 188 infected ones, belonging to 178 organisations. Banking and finance was the biggest group, with 32 organisations.
Victims included HSBC, Equifax, Ledger, Zoom, the BBC, IKEA and Air France-KLM.
The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed cards typed into normal forms, stole cookies and screenshots, and sent exploit kits to older iPhones.
Only 24 of the checked organisations had a Content Security Policy that blocked the payload.
items.summary: On 16 November an attacker added malicious code to Optimizely Web, an A/B-testing tool many big brands load on every page. For about 17 hours it swapped crypto wallet addresses, skimmed card details typed into normal forms, and stole cookies and screenshots. Banking and finance was the most affected sector, with HSBC and ABN AMRO among the victims.
items.title: Hacked Optimizely scripts hit 178 sites, including 32 banks such as HSBC
items.why: MyAmeria probably loads third-party scripts too. This is a strong reason to push for a strict Content Security Policy, hosted payment fields and a list of every vendor script, and it is a good real case for trust and security UX.

body: ## The main idea

Verification means giving an agent a way to prove its work is correct. Osmani says this is what lets one person run many agents at once. Without it, you must read every change yourself, so you can only watch one or two. In internal tests, a separate grader that checked work against a rubric raised success by up to 10 points. Tests are also cheap now, because agents can write them.
## Three kinds of tests

End-to-end (E2E) tests follow a real user path, like adding an item to a cart and paying. They are hard to fool, and when they fail they show the exact step, often with a screenshot. A 'feature map' lists every feature from the user's view, with the expected result. It works as a guide and as a checklist for grading.

Property tests start with a rule that must always be true. For example, a balance never goes below zero, or saving and loading data gives back the same data. A library such as fast-check or Hypothesis then creates thousands of inputs to try to break the rule. Differential tests run the old and new system with the same inputs and compare results. They are best for big migrations.
## How the team works

Verification means running the app, like a QA tester does. The team keeps a 'verify' skill next to the code, and Claude uses it before each commit. Cheap checks (tests, build, linter) run first. A reliability checklist has 39 items, each linked to a past incident. Claude only checks the items that match the change, usually 3 to 10.

A commit gate can block commits that were not reviewed or verified. It has three modes: off, observe and enforce. After two blocks in one session, the next commit goes through, so Claude does not get stuck. Flaky tests (tests that pass or fail at random) may not be skipped or retried until green. If the cause is unknown, the test is deleted with a note.

The team also tests its reviewers. It tracks reverted merges and uses clean, merged changes as a control group. A missed bug becomes a new rule only if the pattern shows up in at least two PRs. Rule files are pruned often so they do not grow forever.
points: Addy Osmani wrote the post on 16 November 2026. About 90% of the Claude Code team's code is written and reviewed by Claude.
The team invests most in three test types: end-to-end, property and differential tests.
If a check still fails after three rounds of fixes, Claude stops and asks a human.
Review rules in REVIEW.md are read from the main branch, so a pull request cannot change its own judge.
Every commit records how it was verified, even when the answer is 'none'.
items.source: Addy Osmani, claude.dev blog (via Hacker News)
items.summary: Addy Osmani explains how the Claude Code team lets agents check their own work. They rely most on end-to-end tests, then property tests (rules that must always be true, like 'a balance never goes negative') and tests that compare the old and new systems. Other rules: an agent stops after three failed tries, review rules come from the main branch so a change cannot edit its own judge, and every commit records how it was checked.
items.title: How the Claude Code team checks AI-written code before it ships
items.why: You are starting to ship MyAmeria features as PRs written with AI agents. Copying a few of these habits, like a 'verify' skill and E2E tests for each flow, will make developers trust your PRs much faster.

body: ## What happened

OpenAI released two new models. Astra is its 'frontier' model, which means its most powerful one. Sol is the cheaper model for daily tasks. Both are in the API. Simon Willison added them to his command-line tool, LLM 0.38, on the same day.
## The prices

Prices are counted in tokens, which are small pieces of text. Astra now costs $8 for a million input tokens and $40 for a million output tokens. That is 80% of the old Astra 6 price, and the same as Claude Fable 5.2. Cached input is text the model has already seen, like a long project history. It now costs $0.40 instead of $1. Willison says this helps a lot in long agent sessions. Sol did not change: $2 in and $10 out.
## The tests

Willison always asks new models to draw a pelican riding a bicycle as an SVG image. Astra at maximum effort made the most detailed drawing he has seen, with feathers and a scarf. That one drawing cost about 89 cents. At lower effort the pictures were simpler but still clear. Sol looked good at high settings, but at its cheapest setting the handlebars were hard to see.

His second test was harder. He asked for a Three.js animation of Yonkers, a city near New York, turning into a giant robot and walking through other parts of the city. Neither model made a convincing robot. He thought Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon did better.

The first reactions are mixed. Astra reportedly scores below Fable 5.2 on several benchmarks, and some users find its way of talking confusing. Developer Theo Browne tested it before launch. He says it manages helper agents well on long tasks. But it asks strange, low-level questions. In one case it stopped for two hours to ask about a file-naming detail.
It is still early. These are first-day tests by a few people, not long-term results.
points: OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra (for the hardest work) and GPT-6.2 Sol (for everyday work) on 17 November 2026.
Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50. Cached input fell from $1 to $0.40.
Sol stays at $2 input and $10 output, the same as Sol 6 and 6.1.
Simon Willison found that neither model beat Claude Fable 5.2 or Gemini 4 Carbon on his 3D animation test.
Theo Browne reports that Astra once stalled for two hours on a question about file names.
items.summary: OpenAI launched two models: Astra for the hardest work and Sol for daily tasks. Astra now costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, the same as Claude Fable 5.2, and Sol stays at $2 and $10. Simon Willison's first tests were mixed: Astra handles long agent tasks well but sometimes stops to ask odd questions, and both models did worse than Fable 5.2 on his animation test.
items.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra (frontier) and GPT-6.2 Sol (everyday)
items.why: You choose models for design and coding work every day. Early tests suggest Astra is not yet better than Fable 5.2 for animation or taste, so it may not be worth changing your setup yet.

body: ## What happened

Microsoft has built its own coding models instead of only using models from OpenAI and others. The two new ones are MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash. Developers who use GitHub Copilot can pick them today. Microsoft says they will also come to OpenRouter, Vercel, OpenCode, Kilo and others soon.

MAI Code 2 is for bigger work: deep debugging, changes across many files, understanding a whole codebase, and building user interfaces. Code 2 Flash is smaller and cheaper. It is for quick jobs, like explaining code, small edits and routine fixes.
## The numbers

Microsoft averaged four coding benchmarks (standard tests for comparing models). On these, Code 2 got 96% of the score of Claude Opus 5.5, at about 5% of its cost. Compared with GPT-6.1 Sol, it got 98% of the score at 40% of the cost. Flash is said to match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of their cost. Note that the prices on the page are a 50% launch discount.

For visual coding, Microsoft ran a blind test. In a blind test, reviewers do not know which model made which result. 258 people compared interfaces, games, charts, 3D scenes and SVG graphics. They chose Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time.
## Limits and caveats

All these numbers come from Microsoft itself, not from independent testers. Microsoft also says results change with the workload, settings and price assumptions. It says clearly that the models are "not yet tuned" for harder problems, such as very long agent tasks.

Microsoft also made MAI Work Flash, a version tuned for Office apps. It says the model uses about 42% fewer input tokens in Word and up to 28% fewer tokens in Teams than the models it replaces or competes with there.
points: Microsoft AI announced MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash on 17 November 2026, at its Ignite event.
Both models are available now in GitHub Copilot. Code 2 Flash is also in a limited preview in Microsoft Foundry.
Microsoft says Code 2 reaches 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's score at 5% of the cost, and 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's score at 40% of the cost.
In a blind test with 258 reviewers, developers preferred Code 2's visual work over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time.
Microsoft says the models are not yet tuned for very long agent tasks or science research.
items.summary: Microsoft released two in-house coding models, MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash, both available now in GitHub Copilot. Microsoft says Code 2 gets about 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's benchmark score at about 5% of the cost. In blind front-end tests, reviewers preferred its UI code over GPT-6 Sol's 64% of the time. Microsoft also says the models are not yet tuned for very long agent tasks.
items.title: Microsoft launches MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot and says it costs far less
items.why: If your developers already use Copilot, this is a cheap model built for UI code that you can try on small, routine front-end tasks.

body: ## What it is

Superhands is a tool for teams that use AI to make designs or code. The problem it tries to solve is common: an AI tool makes a screen, the screen breaks a design rule, and a designer fixes it by hand. Then the next screen has the same mistake. Superhands wants you to fix the rule, not the screen.
## How it works

First, you point it at your existing designs. It studies them and writes down the decisions behind them as guidance. AI agents then use that guidance inside the tools your team already uses. You can see what the agents produce. When something is wrong, you change the guidance in one place, and later outputs follow the fix. The page does not name specific tools it connects to.

Grant MacLennan says AI made execution cheap, but direction was often missing. In other words, it is now easy to make many screens, but hard to make sure they all follow the same thinking. His agency background explains the focus on repeated design corrections.
## Open questions

Users asked good questions that had no answer on the page yet. One asked how it handles fuzzy rules, like tone of voice, and whether agents see examples of bad output or only the rule. A solo SwiftUI developer asked if it can work from app screens alone, without a Figma file or design system. The only review so far gives 4 out of 5. It likes copying whole components, but says copying is slow and there is no separate preview page.

The product is young, but the idea is clear: a design system is no longer only for people. It is also a set of instructions for AI. The team that writes those instructions well can control many AI outputs at once.
points: Superhands launched on Product Hunt with the tagline 'Design the system, not every screen'.
It reads a team's existing designs and turns its design decisions into guidance for AI agents.
It was ranked #10 on the 18 November 2026 leaderboard with 107 points. This is the company's second launch.
It is free to start. The maker is Grant MacLennan, who ran a digital product agency for nine years.
items.summary: Superhands, launched on Product Hunt yesterday, reads a team's existing designs and turns its design decisions into guidance that AI tools follow. When an AI output is wrong, you fix the guidance once instead of fixing every screen. Its tagline is 'design the system, not every screen', and it is free to start.
items.title: Superhands launches: turn your design decisions into rules AI agents follow
items.why: This is very close to your own goal of teaching AI the MyAmeria design system and automating about 85% of design files. Look at how they structure the guidance and compare it with your approach.

body: AI coding agents make software cheap to build and change. So many teams ship first and learn later. But a release only shows what people did, not why they did it. A dashboard can show that users left a flow, but not what confused them. And a bad release reaches real people.
## The method

Alicea calls his answer 'research-in-the-loop'. It has four steps. First, research writes what the release must measure, inside the same requirements document as the product spec. Second, the coding agent builds the feature together with its instrumentation: event logging, dashboards and short in-app surveys. Third, the feature and the measurement ship together. Fourth, researchers study the results, and what they learn shapes the next spec.
## What the research section contains

It has five parts, written in plain language in a file next to the spec, so people and agents can both read it. The expectation is what you think will happen. Signs it worked are target numbers. Signs it caused problems are harm indicators. What to track lists the exact events. When to talk to people sets triggers for interviews.

In the example, a help-desk product lets agents transfer tickets between departments. Success means faster resolution and fewer tickets passing through three or more departments. Problems would be more send-backs and more reopened tickets. If one department sends back many tickets, researchers go and observe there.

Evaluation asks if the change did what you predicted. Investigation asks why people behaved that way. Discovery looks for needs nobody expected, and data cannot replace it. Qualitative work fits through a regular cadence (for example weekly sessions), signals from the data, and big decisions that are hard to undo, like pricing.
## Risks

The numbers do not prove cause. Seasons or staffing changes can also move them. Too many surveys can annoy users and feel like surveillance. Teams may also start choosing only small changes that are easy to measure. To start, Alicea suggests a small step. find where your user data lives and what your agents can access. Write one research section for one release and share it with your product manager and engineers.
points: Tony Alicea of Nielsen Norman Group published the article on 13 November 2026.
The loop has four stages: specify, build and instrument, release, and evaluate and learn.
The spec's research section lists the expectation, signs it worked, signs it caused problems, what to track, and when to talk to people.
Data shows what people did, but not why, so interviews and open-ended discovery are still needed.
The article calls this an emerging idea, not a proven method.
items.summary: Tony Alicea describes 'research-in-the-loop'. Researchers add a research section to the product spec, with a hypothesis, success and harm criteria and what to track. Coding agents then build the logging, dashboards and short in-app surveys together with the feature. After release, the data shows where to run interviews or observation.
items.title: NN/g: build research into the spec when AI ships features in days
items.why: Star ships fast, and kids and parents are hard to recruit. A research section in each spec gives you real numbers for case studies without slowing the team.

items.summary: This newsletter says open design roles have dropped about 61% since 2022, and many roles are filled through referrals before they are posted. It suggests 'side doors': contact recently funded Series A–B companies, write to founders with a specific problem you can solve, and search hybrid titles like Design Engineer. It also says lead roles now outnumber junior roles three to one, and that about half of job posts ask for AI fluency.
items.title: 61% fewer design roles than in 2022: how designers are still getting hired
items.why: For a move to the UK or EU, this supports building relationships and a clear one-line position (for example, kids' and family fintech) before you apply.

body: ## The role

Bitpanda is an investing platform from Vienna, started in 2014. It says it has more than 7 million customers in Europe. People use it to trade crypto, stocks, precious metals and commodities. This role sits in the Web3 team, which designs newer products such as loans backed by your assets in the Bitpanda app, and tokenized structured products in its Vision Wallet. (A tokenized product is a financial product recorded on a blockchain.)

You will design trading and investment screens for mobile and web. A big part of the job is to take hard products, like tokenized derivatives, and make them simple to use. You will also run user research and usability tests, look at user behaviour data, and build and maintain a design system for screens with a lot of data. You work closely with engineers, product managers and the compliance team.
## What they ask for

They want strong Figma and interaction design skills and real experience in crypto, Web3 or complex fintech. They also want someone who uses AI tools every day: to build working coded prototypes fast, and to keep the design system easy for engineers' AI coding tools to use. Experience in regulated, fast-moving teams is listed too.
## Things to check

The post says applicants need an EU passport or a valid work permit for Spain, so visa sponsorship looks unlikely. Benefits include stock options, mental health support, Udemy courses and up to 8 weeks of parent leave. The listing was first posted around 22 October 2026. Salary is not shown.
points: Role: Senior Product Designer in Bitpanda's Web3 team, based in Barcelona, Spain.
Hybrid: 3 days in the office and 2 days at home, plus 25 extra days a year to work from another place.
You need experience in crypto, Web3 or complex fintech, and must already have an EU passport or a work permit.
The team expects you to use AI to build coded prototypes and test them with customers.
items.summary: Bitpanda, a European investing and crypto platform from Vienna, is hiring a Senior Product Designer for its Web3 products in Barcelona. LinkedIn marks the company as fast growing.
items.title: Open role: Senior Product Designer, Web3 at Bitpanda in Barcelona
items.why: It is a senior fintech role in the EU, and your work on banking, payments and investment research for MyInvest fits it well.

body: ## What happened

Satya Nadella, who began his career as a software engineer, spoke for about an hour with Gergely Orosz on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast. The main question was simple: what does software engineering look like when producing code is cheap, but making sure it is correct is not?

Nadella says many teams now build 'software factories': systems of AI agents that do parts of their daily work. His example is the Azure networking team. It deals with more than 500 fibre network operators and built an agent system to handle the emails and processes around them. Orosz notes there is no ready playbook for this, so each team must find its own way.

Nadella also admitted that GitHub Copilot fell behind. When Claude Code moved coding into the command line, the classic code editor became less central in about six months, and Microsoft was not ready. His lesson: one big jump in model quality can change the whole product form very quickly. He advises companies to keep the model, the memory and the 'harness' (the tool around the model) separate, so they can switch providers. He even suggests treating AI agents as an 'insider risk' that needs its own checks.
## Teams and jobs

Microsoft has offered voluntary exits (paid packages to leave) to most of its engineers, which has never happened before. Orosz reads this as a sign of large reorganisations: smaller teams, changed roles, and new AI jobs such as forward-deployed engineers. Nadella said not every team has become AI-native yet. Junior hiring has slowed while teams balance people costs against token budgets, but he expects it to come back. Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University also started PRAISE, a mentoring programme borrowed from nursing, where senior engineers coach newer ones on using AI with good judgement.

Nadella says verification is not solved. If you ask a model to review code, it can cheat, for example by deleting failing tests so the rest pass. Loops that learn from production data also need their own checks. The talk ended with no clear answer.
## What comes next

Nadella expects 'hybrid intelligence': cheap local models on laptops for simple tasks and stronger cloud models for hard ones. His personal advice is to do more, learn more and spend time inside teams that already work this way.
points: Gergely Orosz of The Pragmatic Engineer interviewed Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella; the episode came out on 16 November 2026.
For the first time ever, Microsoft offered voluntary exits to most of its software engineers; they can accept until December.
Nadella admits junior and new-graduate hiring has slowed, but he calls it a temporary phase while teams reorganise.
He says checking AI-written code (verification) is still an unsolved problem.
His advice: use AI more, talk about it less, and be hands-on.
items.summary: In a Pragmatic Engineer interview, Microsoft's CEO says teams are building 'software factories' and many teams are getting smaller, while new AI teams form. Microsoft has offered voluntary exits to most software engineers for the first time, and junior hiring has slowed for now. He says writing code is now cheap but checking it is still an unsolved problem, and his main advice is to spend more hands-on time with AI.
items.title: Satya Nadella: teams shrink, new AI teams form, and checking code is the hard part
items.why: This shows how big companies are reshaping teams around AI. It is useful context when you discuss team structure and your own role at Ameriabank.

body: ## The basic idea

A stablecoin is a digital token that keeps a fixed value, usually one US dollar. A stablecoin-linked card looks like a normal Visa or Mastercard to the shop. The difference is behind the scenes: the money that backs the card is held, and settled, in stablecoins instead of only in bank money.

Taylor first explains the normal chain. The shop's payment provider sends your tap through the card network to the issuer, which approves or declines. Later, the network adds up what everyone owes, and the issuer pays. Several roles sit behind a card: the program manager sets rules, the principal member is allowed by the network to run the program, the issuer processor moves the data and updates balances, and the BIN sponsor provides the card numbers. Monzo does all of this itself. KAST, a newer wallet, uses Rain for most of it.
## Going to many countries at once

Normally, to launch cards in a new country you need a local bank, a pre-filled account, a way to change money into dollars, and you must follow that country's bank holidays. With a dollar stablecoin program, one global BIN sponsor and program manager can cover many markets. The user gets one dollar balance and a card that works everywhere, which matters in places where dollars are hard to get.

Banks close on weekends, but people keep spending. So issuers must put money aside before long holidays. In Taylor's example, $1M of daily spending needs about $4M set aside for a four-day weekend. Because the networks now accept stablecoin settlement every day, the issuer can settle daily and keep a much smaller buffer. Spread across five markets, five pots of $800k could become one $1M balance.
## New features for users

Balances can earn yield (interest) next to spending money; KAST reportedly offers 4% to 7%. Rain bought Ansa, which lets wallets pay at normal shop terminals and earn rewards, and Uptop, a rewards system. Taylor also imagines global fan cards for clubs like Manchester United. He calls the ideal a 'T-shaped' program: wide across many markets and deep in features.

The brand still owns support, fraud, disputes and funding, even if a provider runs the technology. Big local banks may find stablecoin funding slower or more expensive. Remember that Rain paid for this piece.
points: Simon Taylor's Fintech Brainfood piece (17 November 2026) is a paid partnership with Rain, a stablecoin card provider.
Visa and Mastercard now let issuers settle in stablecoins on weekends and holidays.
Example: a $4M cash buffer for a four-day weekend across five markets could shrink to one shared $1M balance, freeing $3M.
KAST reportedly pays 4% to 7% yield on balances; Nubank's Nu Global aims at 35 markets.
The author says large domestic banks may gain little, because they already settle cheaply in normal money.
items.summary: Simon Taylor explains how stablecoin-linked cards let one card program run in many countries, with fewer local banking partners. They can also settle with card networks on weekends, so issuers need less cash set aside. For users, this could mean one global dollar balance, interest earned next to spending, and rewards at any shop.
items.title: Fintech Brainfood: what stablecoin-linked cards make possible
items.why: It helps you understand where card and wallet products are going, which is useful for future MyAmeria wallet and card ideas.

body: ## What happened

Alpha Bank, based in Athens, has a new identity by Pentagram's London office. The bank collects art and old coins, and since 1972 its logo has been based on an ancient silver coin from the island of Aegina. Pentagram kept this story but made the whole brand feel warmer and more modern, for both young professionals and wealthy clients.
## One symbol drives everything

The team redrew the coin symbol. They kept the line through the middle of the coin and placed it in a round frame. They also kept small unevenness from the original coin, so it still feels hand-made and historic. The key design decision: almost everything else comes from this one shape. The wordmark, typeface, icons, signs, floor numbers and patterns all borrow from it.

Alpha Sans is a custom font with five weights, in both Greek and Latin letters. It was made with Tom Baber, and its shapes also echo the symbol. A second font, Alpha Text, handles smaller body copy. Designing both alphabets together matters for a bank in a non-Latin country: the brand looks the same in both languages.
## Colour as a system

The core is the existing Alpha Blue, white and a lighter Galazio Blue. Secondary colours are Thalassi Turquoise, Heritage Pink and Alpha Gold. Sub-brands like Business and Private Banking use different colours, so customers know where they are. Five bright extra colours are only for digital elements such as infographics. This keeps the main brand calm while giving data screens enough contrast and variety.

The icons were drawn to match the new symbol and to work at every size, from big posters to tiny app interface icons. Patterns made from parts of the symbol and wordmark can be loud graphics or quiet textures. Photos show everyday people and places with a soft, blurred background.
Simple Revolution wrote the strategy, with the idea 'Building progress, together'. Other studios designed the branches and signs. The first new branch opened in Kolonaki, a smart district of Athens.
points: Pentagram London, led by partner Domenic Lippa, redesigned Alpha Bank, a Greek bank founded in 1879 with more than 200 branches.
The symbol comes from a silver coin from Aegina (479-456 BCE); the first logo based on it appeared in 1972.
New custom typeface Alpha Sans has five weights in Greek and Latin, made with type designer Tom Baber.
Business and Private Banking get their own colours, and five bright colours are kept only for digital use like charts.
The project was announced on 12 November 2026.
items.summary: Domenic Lippa's team at Pentagram London rebuilt Alpha Bank's identity. They redrew the coin-based symbol, created a custom Greek and Latin typeface called Alpha Sans, and made a colour system with separate colours for business and private banking. There is also an icon set that works down to small app sizes, and five bright colours only for digital elements like charts.
items.title: Pentagram redraws Greece's Alpha Bank around its 1972 coin symbol
items.why: It is a rare top-studio case of a bank brand built for digital. Study how the icons and the digital colours work as a system, and compare them with your MyAmeria tokens.

body: ## What happened

Major League Baseball asked Mother Design to give its brand more focus and energy and to reach newer fans. Baseball has more than a century of history and is closely linked to American identity. The studio felt the old design system did not use this history well, so it went back to the sport's past for material.
## Starting with letters

Instead of starting with a logo or a colour, the team started with typography. They made a family of five custom typefaces. The article names three. MLB Franklin, by Nick Sherman, reworks Franklin Gothic, a typeface that feels like 19th-century American printing. MLB Clarendon, by David Jonathan Ross and Bethany Heck, is a narrow slab serif (letters with thick, block-like feet) based on Clarendon from 1845, a style long used in baseball. MLB Block, by Skye Dillon, has eight-sided letters like those seen at old stadiums such as Ebbets Field and on uniform numbers.

The colours are taken from the teams' own colours and their stadiums, then reduced to a bright set that can stand for every club. The graphic tools come from the game itself: the five-sided home plate, base lines and scoreboard lines, the round ball, a bird's-eye view of the field, and old baseball cards and uniforms. The system is built to work across platforms, from social media posts to tickets.
The well-known MLB logo, with its player silhouette, was not changed. That is a common choice in a refresh: keep the most recognised part, and change the system around it.
## The lesson

The method is to find what is already special in a brand's own past and turn it into tools, instead of following current trends. Each piece here, from letter shapes to lines, has a clear source in the sport.
points: Mother Design refreshed Major League Baseball's brand and design system; It's Nice That reported it on 16 November 2026.
The work started from type: five custom typefaces based on historic lettering.
Named faces: MLB Franklin (Nick Sherman), MLB Clarendon (David Jonathan Ross and Bethany Heck) and MLB Block (Skye Dillon).
The colours come from the 30 clubs' own colours; the classic MLB logo silhouette did not change.
items.summary: Mother Design refreshed Major League Baseball's brand starting from typography. The custom faces include a Franklin Gothic rework, a condensed Clarendon slab serif and an octagonal 'Block' face taken from old stadiums and uniforms. The colours come from the clubs' own colours, and graphic tools come from the field's geometry, while the logo stays the same.
items.title: Mother Design refreshes MLB with five custom typefaces from baseball history
items.why: It shows how to update an old brand by digging into its own history instead of following trends. You can use the same idea when you develop Star's visual style.

body: ## The problem

Coding agents can run commands on your computer. A mistake, or a prompt injection (hidden text that tricks the model into doing something bad), could damage files or leak data. Willison wanted a safer way to try new models, especially local ones, without that worry.
## The pattern

In most setups, the whole agent runs inside a sandbox (a closed, isolated space). In the 'external sandbox' pattern, the agent stays outside. Only the code it wants to run is sent into the sandbox. The agent calls a small API on your own machine, the sandbox runs the code, and the result comes back. So the agent can think and plan freely, but it cannot touch your real system when it executes something.

Willison released three demo versions. The first is a Node.js server that uses v86 to run Alpine Linux (a very small Linux) inside WebAssembly. The second is a Python server that runs Alpine Linux in Apple Containers, so it is for Macs. The third is a Python server built on Microsoft's Quicksand library, which packs QEMU (a machine emulator) and Alpine Linux into one Python package. All three offer the same localhost API, so you can switch between them without changing the agent.

There is an optional proxy with an allow-list: you decide which websites the sandboxed code may talk to. A web page lets you edit this list while the sandbox runs and see recent traffic. There is also a credential replacement feature. The code can make real, signed-in API calls, but the agent itself never sees the secret key. The short post does not explain how this works inside.
## What is still unknown
These are demos, not finished products. A longer write-up on the Prime Radiant blog may cover the threat model and the limits. You can point Pi, Claude Code or Codex at the sandbox to try it.
points: Simon Willison wrote about the 'external sandbox' pattern on 17 November 2026.
The agent runs normally, but any code it wants to run goes to an isolated sandbox through a localhost API.
Three versions: v86 (Linux in WebAssembly, Node.js), Apple Containers (Python), and Microsoft's Quicksand library (Python with QEMU).
Extras: an optional allow-list of websites the code may reach, and credential replacement so the agent never holds your secret keys.
Works with Pi, Claude Code or Codex.
items.summary: Simon Willison describes the 'external sandbox' pattern. The agent runs normally, but any code it wants to run is sent to an isolated sandbox. He released three versions of the sandbox, with an optional list of allowed websites and a way to call APIs without giving the agent your secret keys.
items.title: Simon Willison: run your coding agent's code in a separate sandbox
items.why: When your agents write and run code for the bank's apps, keeping them away from real secrets and your main machine is basic safety, and the security team will ask about it.

body: ## What happened

On the morning of 17 November (US time), many Apple services stopped working. People could not connect or sign in. Some were suddenly signed out of iCloud on their iPhone or Mac, and when they tried to sign back in, they saw verification failures or an 'unknown error'. The App Store would not load or download apps. Some new or reset devices could not reach Apple's activation servers.
## Who was affected

Problems hit iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, Apple Music, Apple Support and iPhone activation. App developers had trouble with App Store Connect, the site where they manage and release apps. Reports said Apple's own shops and offices were affected as well.

For a while, Apple's public System Status page still said everything was working, while the outage-tracking site Downdetector showed many user reports. Apple later listed the issues on its normal and developer status pages.
## The cause

In an update, 9to5Mac shared Apple's statement, reported by Mark Gurman of Bloomberg: an internal update had caused outages that morning, and many systems were back. Apple said it was not a cyberattack. Consumer services came back first. Developer services were still having problems at the time of the update. The article does not say exactly when the outage started or fully ended.
points: On Tuesday 17 November 2026, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, Apple Music, Apple Support and device activation had problems.
Users were signed out of iCloud on iPhone and Mac and got 'unknown errors' when signing back in.
Developers could not use App Store Connect; Apple stores and offices were reportedly hit too.
Apple later said an internal update caused the outages and that it was not a cyberattack.
items.summary: On Tuesday, many Apple services went down, including iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay and App Store Connect. Users were signed out of iCloud and could not sign back in. Apple later said an internal update caused the problems and that it was not a cyberattack.
items.title: Apple outage hits iCloud, App Store and Apple Pay
items.why: Apple Pay and App Store problems reach banking apps too. Think about what MyAmeria shows users when a platform service it depends on fails.

items.summary: Four UK regulators (the CMA, FCA, ICO and Ofcom) sent a joint letter on 16 November about AI agents that act for customers, like booking or paying. They ask companies to talk to them early and add safeguards before launch. They name scams, data sharing that goes further than people expect, and misleading recommendations as the main risks. No new rules yet: they say current law already applies.
items.title: UK regulators warn ministers: personal AI agents are coming, check risks before launch
items.why: This is the rulebook forming for agent features in UK banking. If you design an AI money assistant for MyAmeria or Star, consent, limits and clear explanations are what UK fintech employers will ask you about.

items.summary: Andrew Chung shows a 'two-speed' problem: AI speeds up design and code, but only 30% of people surveyed said it sped up testing. He gives a simple routine in three steps: find issues early (put focus order, labels and states into the design system and the files AI tools read), fix them while context is fresh (use AI for draft fixes, then check them by hand), and prove it (keep test notes in each PR).
items.title: Smashing: AI made building faster, but accessibility testing is falling behind
items.why: You plan to ship app code with AI agents. This is a ready checklist for adding accessibility to those PRs and to your design-system docs, which EU banking roles now expect.

items.source: San Francisco Chronicle, via Yahoo News
items.summary: Anthropic, the maker of Claude, set its share price at $83, above its planned $70–78 range, because demand was several times larger than the shares on offer. That values the company at about $1.5 trillion. Shares trade under the ticker ANT from Thursday, 19 November.
items.title: Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 a share; trading on Nasdaq starts today
items.why: Claude is a core tool in your daily AI workflow. A public Anthropic will face more pressure on pricing and product speed, which affects the tools you build your design-to-code process on.

items.summary: Versine lets AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude send and request money through an MCP connection. Money only moves after you approve with a passkey, unless you allow small payments to trusted contacts within limits you set. Adding a trusted contact also needs your passkey, so the agent cannot add one alone.
items.title: Versine launches 'Venmo for agents': your AI sets up payments, you approve with a passkey
items.why: A clear, real example of agent-payment UX: approval screens, spending limits and per-person trust levels. Good pattern study for any AI feature in MyAmeria, and a safer model to think about for kids in Star.

items.summary: Two Harvard PhD researchers looked at about 726,000 workers in 718 companies. With AI coding tools, lines of code rose about 30% and pull requests 23%, but finished tasks shipped to users did not measurably rise. The time to review and merge a PR grew by 49%. It is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed, and the data partner sells engineering analytics. It is trending on Hacker News today.
items.title: Harvard study: AI agents wrote 30% more code, but finished work did not grow
items.why: If you send AI-written PRs to the MyAmeria developers, review time is the real bottleneck. Small, well-explained PRs with tests will get merged; big ones will wait.

items.summary: Nielsen updates his 2024 essay and grades his own predictions (3 right, 1 mostly right, 1 wrong). His point: AI vendors now sell finished work, like a resolved support ticket, and charge per result instead of per seat. He argues that designing and checking the 'meter' (what counts as a finished job) is now a core UX task, because failed or fake results stay the buyer's problem.
items.title: Jakob Nielsen: 'service as a software' is arriving faster than he predicted
items.why: Banks will buy and build AI services priced this way. Knowing how to define a 'done' outcome and show it honestly to users is product-strategy thinking that senior roles test for.

items.source: Chris Nguyen (UX Playbook), via rectangles newsletter
items.summary: Chris Nguyen (rectangles, UX Playbook) shares the method he used to go from being fired to Head of Design. Write one 'From → To' sentence, then set milestones that change your skills, visibility or responsibility (not just 'take a course'). Give each milestone actions, resources, people who can help, and a real deadline, and update the map every 6–12 months.
items.title: How to make a career journey map: a step-by-step guide for designers
items.why: Your goal (UK move, Global Talent visa, top designer) has many parts. A map like this turns it into dated milestones, such as an award entry or a published case study.

items.summary: Daniel Stenberg, who maintains curl, looked at projects where AI agents turned about 185,000 lines of C into about 340,000 lines of Rust. In the same three weeks the real curl team merged over 300 commits and fixed about 200 bugs, which the copies don't have. He asks if the clones can keep up. Simon Willison highlighted the post.
items.title: curl's creator: AI rewrites of curl in Rust are already falling behind
items.why: A useful reminder for your own AI-coding work: generating code is the easy part, keeping it maintained and in sync is the hard part. Worth saying in interviews about your AI workflow.

items.summary: A UK government review, after almost 7,000 bank branches closed since 2015, suggests a legal duty for banks to keep in-person services. It also floats measuring banks by share of transactions, not current accounts, which would likely include digital banks like Revolut, Monzo and Starling. The Treasury expects to bring in the law in 2028.
items.title: UK may make Revolut and Monzo help pay for high-street banking hubs
items.why: Shows how UK regulation shapes digital-bank products and costs. Useful context if you interview with UK neobanks.

items.summary: North Design rebranded the Sainsbury Museum and Art Centre in Norwich. The logo uses three nested rectangles taken from Foster's sketch of the building's steel frames, inspired by Otl Aicher's 'intelligent geometry'. A custom monospaced font has two modes: normal spacing for signs and uneven, expressive spacing for posters and digital work.
items.title: North Design turns a 1970s Norman Foster sketch into the Sainsbury Centre's new brand
items.why: A good lesson for design systems: one typeface with a 'functional' and an 'expressive' mode. You could use the same idea for MyAmeria (calm) versus Star (playful).

items.summary: Stark released a plugin that lets Codex scan Figma files, code, Storybook, mobile apps and live sites for accessibility problems, then suggest code-level fixes. It has five role-based skills, for design, front-end, back-end, mobile and program management. It was already in Claude's connector directory since August.
items.title: Stark's accessibility checker now works inside OpenAI's Codex and ChatGPT
items.why: Pairs with the Smashing article: you could run accessibility checks in the same AI tools you use to build MyAmeria screens, and show it in a case study.

items.summary: A review of 2026 data says a randomised experiment found about 40% fewer clicks on searches that showed an AI Overview. Overviews now appear on about 61% of tracked keywords, up from about 6% in 2024. Google says total clicks are stable but has not shared numbers. Most data comes from SEO vendors and US desktop users.
items.title: Study roundup: Google's AI answers cut clicks to websites by about 40%
items.why: People find answers inside AI now, not on websites. For bank marketing and help pages, design for being quoted by AI, and track it, not only page visits.

items.summary: Brand New posted the new logo and identity for Caixa, a Brazilian bank, designed by the studio Tátil Design. The post shows before-and-after logos and examples in use; the full written review is for subscribers only.
items.title: Brazilian bank Caixa gets a new logo and identity by Tátil Design
items.why: A large bank rebrand to study next to your own MyAmeria work: compare how they handle colour, logo and app use.

items.summary: Brad Frost says AI makes a weak design system worse, so fix the base first. He shared a set of free agent skills. The main one, /ds-inspection, reads your code, Figma library and docs (through Figma Console MCP), gives a score out of 100 and a ranked list of fixes for quality, accessibility, design-code match and AI readiness. One team went from 70 to 83.
items.title: Brad Frost releases a free AI skill that grades your design system
items.why: You are teaching AI the MyAmeria design system right now. Run this on MyAmeria before you automate file creation, so the agents copy a clean system, not its gaps.

items.summary: Fraud company Feedzai added a way for banks to see when an AI agent, not a person, is using an account. It links the customer, their device and the bank ("device binding"), so the bank knows who the agent works for. Banks can then allow, challenge or block each agent action, and skip repeat logins for agents the customer already trusts.
items.title: Feedzai lets banks spot, allow or block AI agents inside customer accounts
items.why: Kids and parents will soon send agents into MyAmeria and Star too. This gives you a real model for the UX: how to show a parent which agent did what, and how to say yes or no.

items.summary: Anthropic (ticker ANT) started trading on 19 November. The first trade was $111.50, well above the $83 IPO price. The stock then fell back and closed at $97.17, still 17% up. About 832 million shares changed hands.
items.title: Anthropic's first day on Nasdaq: opens 34% above IPO price, closes up 17%
items.why: Claude is a core tool in your 80–90% AI workflow. A public, well-funded Anthropic means faster model and tool releases you will feel in your daily design and code work.

items.summary: Gemini 4 Neon sits between Google's biggest model (Carbon) and its fastest (Hydrogen). Google says it ranks first on an independent coding-agent index and handles files, charts and video in a 1-million-token memory. It costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens.
items.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon, a fast model that tops a coding-agent ranking
items.why: You ship Android and iOS code with agents. A strong, cheaper coding model is worth a test run against your current setup on one real MyAmeria task.

items.summary: Tecla launched on Product Hunt. Instead of a chat box, it pulls tasks from Slack, email and meetings into a to-do list, each with its context. You press "run" on the items you want the agent to do. No prompts needed.
items.title: Tecla: an AI agent whose whole interface is a to-do list
items.why: A clear agent-UX pattern: the list is the control and the "run" button is the consent. Useful thinking for how a child or parent could hand tasks to an agent in Star.

items.summary: Anthropic says a team of Claude agents worked in the background for about six weeks on 22 hard physics questions and cracked two. One result was checked by an independent physicist, the other was formally proved with software. Neither changes daily life, but it shows long, unattended agent work.
items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open black-hole physics problems in six weeks
items.why: It shows where agents are heading: many copies checking each other over weeks. That is the same idea behind your plan to let agents build features and hand you PRs to review.

items.summary: Onlook (on Hacker News today) lets you design inside your running Next.js and Tailwind app. You drag elements, change styles from a toolbar and manage design tokens, and the code updates live. It has branches for design variations and is free under Apache 2.0.
items.title: Onlook: an open-source, Figma-like editor that edits real React code
items.why: It fits your goal of designers shipping code. Worth a look as a way to tweak UI in code without waiting for a developer.

items.source: Brand New (UnderConsideration); details from Fast Company
items.summary: Nubank refreshed its brand for its move into the US. It kept its famous purple but added new secondary colours, a custom font called Nu Sans that works big in ads and small in the app, playful illustrations and bouncy motion. The reason: purple is now everywhere in fintech, so Nu needed more than one colour to stand out.
items.title: Brand New reviews Nubank's new identity by Koto and its in-house team
items.why: A fintech brand that is playful but still trusted is exactly Star's challenge. Study how they use type and motion, not only colour, to feel unique.

items.summary: Airalo, a fast-growing eSIM travel app, is hiring a Senior Product Designer in Barcelona. It appeared in your LinkedIn job alert for senior product design roles there.
items.title: Open role: Senior Product Designer at Airalo in Barcelona
items.why: Barcelona is on your EU list, and Airalo is a consumer mobile app with payments, close to your MyAmeria experience.

items.summary: Clearleft's UX London returns on 6–8 July 2027 at CodeNode in central London. A small batch of super-early-bird tickets is on sale now. Speakers are not announced yet; topics include research, interface design and design systems.
items.title: UX London 2027 opens super-early-bird tickets (6–8 July, London)
items.why: A good target for meeting UK design leaders, and later for speaking. Talks at known UK events help build evidence for a Global Talent visa.

items.summary: Dave, a US money app, asked regulators for a national bank charter to create Dave Bank. With it, Dave could hold deposits and give credit itself instead of through a partner bank. Nubank and Upstart made similar moves this year.
items.title: US app Dave applies to become a real bank
items.why: More fintech apps are becoming full banks. Bank-grade apps like MyAmeria will face rivals with startup-style UX and the same licences.

items.summary: Designer Callum Abbott explains how he builds magazines around type. He keeps the same fonts every issue and changes the layout instead, picks cheaper fonts that fit the mood, and uses letters in surprising ways, like see-through coloured letters over photos.
items.title: Callum Abbott: "A good designer can make a free font look expensive"
items.why: Practical type lessons for your token and typography work: fewer fonts, more layout ideas.

items.summary: Yale professor Julián Posada argues that AI training platforms hire doctors, lawyers and designers at high rates, then cut pay or drop projects suddenly. One designer's tagging job ended and came back days later at a lower rate under a new name.
items.title: Rest of World: AI is turning skilled jobs into low-paid gig work
items.why: A reminder to grow skills AI can't easily replace, like product judgement, strategy and leadership, instead of only execution.

items.summary: A UK court said the government must confirm it sent Apple a secret order to weaken iCloud encryption. The ruling does not say the order is illegal; a full hearing is expected in 2027. Apple already removed its strongest iCloud protection for new UK users.
items.title: UK tribunal forces the government to admit its secret Apple encryption order
items.why: If you move to the UK, this affects how private your data is there. It is also a live case on privacy versus security, a key theme in banking trust UX.

items.summary: Citi added a new section to its online terms. If you give a third-party AI agent access to your account, Citi treats everything the agent does as authorized by you, even mistakes, even if your password later leaks. Transfers the agent starts count as yours, even if they go against what you told it. PNC, Citizens, JPMorgan and Bank of America have made similar changes. Citi's own AI tools are excluded.
items.title: US banks say you're liable for whatever an AI agent does with your login
items.why: Banks are drawing a hard line between 'our agent' and 'their agent'. For MyAmeria, this is a cue to design clear in-app agent permissions and a visible way to cut off outside agents, so trust stays with the bank's own app.

items.summary: In a study of developers who use coding agents, only about half said they read permission requests carefully. Many approve by habit after seeing many look-alike requests. Nielsen suggests three levels: allow read-only and sandboxed actions silently, ask only for writes and deletes (and say what will change and whether it can be undone), and block sensitive data by default. Fire each prompt in context, one at a time.
items.title: Jakob Nielsen: people approve AI agent requests on reflex, so ask less often
items.why: A clear checklist you can apply to any MyAmeria or Star flow where an agent or a parent approves an action. 'Show what changes and if it can be undone' is directly useful for payment confirmations.

items.summary: NN/g gave an AI model the same design task twice: once with about 100 raw user comments, once with a researcher's summary of findings and recommendations. Designs built from the summary met more of the quality checklist, about 78% vs 70%. Raw comments made the AI miss important needs, like keeping the order total visible at every checkout step.
items.title: NN/g test: AI makes better designs from research findings than from raw user comments
items.why: You are automating most design-file creation with AI. This shows the input matters: feed agents written findings and decisions, not raw feedback dumps, and treat research docs as written for two readers, your team and the AI.

items.summary: Meta employees reported internally that Muse, Meta's AI agent, showed them information from other accounts, such as childcare requests, orders and bank balances. One employee said it reminded her about a Signal message even though she had not given it access to that app. Meta says employees test versions that the public doesn't use.
items.title: Meta's Muse agent reportedly mixed up users' chats, showing others' bank balances
items.why: A real example of how one privacy failure in an agent can break trust overnight. Useful evidence when you argue for strict data limits in any AI feature inside a banking app.

items.summary: Google added 'computer use' to the Gemini Mac app. It can fill out forms, sort files and build slides by working in apps and websites in the background. You watch a live preview in the chat, keep using your screen, and can pause, stop or approve actions. It's US-only and English-only for paid plans for now.
items.title: Gemini for Mac can now use your apps and files for you
items.why: Live preview, pause and approve are becoming the standard pattern for agent UX. Worth studying before you design any 'do it for me' feature.

items.summary: A job listing that Bloomberg spotted shows Apple is building an agent that can use apps, browse and write code, privately. At the same time, macOS 27.3 will add warnings that discourage users from giving third-party agents full control of a Mac. The project is still early.
items.title: Apple is reportedly building its own Mac agent and adding warnings for rival agents
items.why: Platforms are adding consent warnings for agents. Your iOS designs will soon need to fit Apple's new agent permission patterns, so watch how they look.

items.summary: Signal now blocks screenshots inside the app on iOS 27. On Android, it turns on 'screen security' when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen. Users can turn this off. Signal admits the protection has gaps and asks Apple, Google and Microsoft to give apps a proper way to opt out.
items.title: Signal blocks phone AI assistants from reading its screen by default
items.why: Banking screens show balances and card data. Signal's approach is a model for deciding when MyAmeria should hide content from system AI agents, and how to explain that choice to users.

items.summary: Kirey España is hiring two designers in the Barcelona area: a Senior Product Designer (UX/UI) for mobile apps, and a Product AI Designer focused on design systems. Both came through your LinkedIn job alert this week, and the company is marked as fast growing.
items.title: Kirey Barcelona hiring a 'Product AI Designer: Design System Expert' and a mobile Senior PD
