items.why: The second role matches what you are doing now: teaching AI a design system to automate design files. A good EU option, and a test of how you pitch that work in your portfolio.

items.summary: N26 added Aura, its fifth and most expensive tier. It includes unlimited airport lounge access, better rewards, free trades and bundled subscriptions like Amazon Prime and Google AI Pro, plus a mirror-finish ceramic card. It costs €10 less than Revolut Ultra and is only in Germany for now.
items.title: N26 launches Aura, a €55-a-month premium account
items.why: Shows how neobanks now sell premium tiers as bundles of lifestyle perks. Useful context for how MyAmeria presents paid plans and how tier comparison screens are designed.

items.summary: Visa expanded Agentic Ready to merchants and payment providers. Participants get a shared way to test how payments started by AI agents are recognized, checked and processed on their current systems. More than 175 card issuers in 45 markets already take part.
items.title: Visa opens its 'Agentic Ready' testing program to Stripe, Adyen, PayPal and 140+ others
items.why: Agent payments are moving from demos to real testing at scale. MyAmeria will likely need a screen for approving or limiting agent purchases; start collecting patterns now.

items.summary: Canva is slowly rolling out a setting for Free and Pro users that turns off its AI features in one place. A separate option hides AI-generated templates in search. Basic tools like background remover stay on. On team plans, admins control AI access.
items.title: Canva adds one switch to turn off its AI features
items.why: A sign that 'AI optional' is becoming a product feature. For the kids' app, a parent-level switch for AI features could be a trust point to consider.

items.summary: Developer Christian Ekrem argues that reviewing code is a skill that fades without practice, like music or writing. Reading mostly AI-written code speeds up the decline. His advice: keep solving the hard parts yourself, and don't let AI replace the effort that builds skill.
items.title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
items.why: Your plan is to ship Android and iOS code with AI agents as PRs. To review agent output well, keep writing some code by hand, not only prompting.

items.summary: Elena Verna says that in fast markets, growth comes mostly from the market's momentum. A company's job is to build a 'raft' that catches it: a loved product, fast shipping, a lean team using AI, trust, social sharing by founders and staff, and bold bets you can change quickly.
items.title: Elena Verna's 'Whitewater' framework: how Lovable grew so fast
items.why: Good language for strategy talks at Ameriabank and for explaining how a small design team can move fast with AI.

items.summary: Docker updated its brand and its whale mascot, Moby, with help from brand firm Motto. The CMO says the company is now about securely running AI agents, not only containers, and the brand needed to show that. They kept Moby because the community knows it.
items.title: Docker redraws its Moby whale as it shifts from containers to AI agents
items.why: An example of updating a beloved mascot instead of replacing it. Useful thinking for the Star characters as the product grows.

items.summary: Mozilla says Apple's rules for other browser engines in the EU and Japan are so hard to meet that no one has launched one. For example, using its own engine would force Firefox to ship a second app that users must install and move data to by hand.
items.title: Mozilla: three years on, still no non-Apple browser engine on iPhone
items.why: iOS platform rules still shape what any app can build. Useful background for the iOS side of MyAmeria and for following how EU rules play out.

items.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a note saying he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the most famous open problems in maths, plus a version that covers the 'generalized' form. The proof is written in Lean, a language that lets computers check every step. Terence Tao lists it with other new AI-assisted results and says it is 'very early days': the proof is huge, made mostly by an internal AI model, and experts still need time to understand it.
items.title: Mathematician says he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
items.why: If it holds, this is the strongest sign yet that AI can do deep original work, not just tasks. It is also a lesson in trust: the claim matters because a machine-checkable proof exists, and the same idea (show checkable evidence, not just output) applies to the AI features you design.

items.summary: Anne Boden, who founded Starling Bank, unveiled Lockwood. Customers get personal AI assistants that pay bills, cancel subscriptions and buy repeat gifts, but only inside limits the customer sets. It plans an e-money licence in 2027, a full bank in 2028, a current account with no lending, and a waiting list is already open.
items.title: Starling founder Anne Boden launches Lockwood, a UK bank built for AI agents
items.why: This is a UK bank whose whole product is agent UX: limits, approvals and undo. It is exactly the space where a designer with banking and kids'-money experience can stand out in the UK market you are targeting.

items.summary: Stitch Loop is an experimental 'product agent' from Google Labs that launched on Product Hunt this weekend. It connects to your GitHub repo and live product data (logs, user behaviour, feedback), suggests fixes, builds the one you pick in a sandbox and opens a pull request that a human must review. It has built-in loops for security, speed and accessibility, and keeps watching the metric after release.
items.title: Google Labs' Stitch Loop finds product problems, codes the fix and opens a PR
items.why: It works almost exactly like your plan to ship MyAmeria features as PRs the dev team reviews. Watch how Google handles the 'human approves the merge' step and the after-launch metric; both are good ideas to borrow for your own workflow and case study.

items.summary: METR, a group that measures how long a task AI can finish, updated its famous chart with longer and more open-ended tasks. Models keep improving on work that can be checked automatically, like code and maths. But on judgment tasks, such as designing useful AI tests or scoring arguments, they still fall short of people.
items.title: METR's updated chart: AI is great at checkable tasks, still weak at judgment
items.why: This is evidence for where your value as a designer sits: taste, judgment and deciding what is good. Use it when you explain to hiring managers why a senior designer still matters in an AI-heavy team.

items.summary: The FT is hiring a senior designer to evolve Origami, its design system for web and mobile. The role asks for design-system and component experience, advanced Figma (variables, tokens), basic HTML and CSS for prototypes, accessibility knowledge, and it lists AI and agent skills. It is hybrid at the FT's London office; salary and visa support are not stated.
items.title: Open role: Senior Product Designer, Design Systems at the Financial Times, London
items.why: It matches your strongest story: you built the MyAmeria design system from scratch and are teaching AI to use it. Even if you don't apply now, it is a clear checklist of what London teams want from a design-system senior.

items.summary: Maria Rosala gives a clear overview of four methods: usability tests, interviews, field studies and diary studies. Start from your question: tests find design problems, the others explore needs and habits. Watch people when accuracy matters, use diaries for experiences that last days or weeks, and test with about five people per group, fix, then test again.
items.title: NN/g: how to pick the right qualitative research method
items.why: A practical guide for testing MyAmeria Star with kids and parents. A diary study over a week of pocket money, for example, could show habits a single session never would.

items.summary: On Thursday the S&P 500 fell 2% for a sixth losing day and the Nasdaq dropped 2.3%, even as Anthropic's shares closed 17% above their IPO price on day one. Investors fear AI is a bubble, worry about interest rates and regulation, and were shaken by Jensen Huang leaving Nvidia. Techmeme-listed reports say the slide continued on Friday, with Anthropic falling on its second day.
items.title: AI stock sell-off deepens: S&P 500 has its longest losing run since 2024
items.why: When markets cool on AI, budgets and hiring can tighten. It is a good moment to make sure your portfolio shows business results, not just AI experiments.

items.summary: Experts often can't explain how they decide, because much of their skill is pattern-based and unspoken. Cutler argues that context is built through shared work (watching, pairing, asking), not only through documents. His tips: define the decision first, have the experts review what is written about them, and sometimes just hold a meeting instead of building a bigger AI context setup.
items.title: John Cutler: writing context documents for AI does not capture real expertise
items.why: You are teaching AI your design system. This is a reminder to record the 'why' behind decisions and to have teammates review it, or the AI will copy the look but miss the judgment.

items.summary: Qonto, which serves over 750,000 small businesses and freelancers in eight European countries, received a full bank licence from French regulators. It can now offer deposits protected up to €100,000, and plans credit lines, loans and invoice financing across Europe in the first half of 2027.
items.title: French business neobank Qonto gets a full banking licence
items.why: Qonto is one of the EU fintechs on your 'after the UK' list. A move into lending means new, hard product flows (applications, limits, repayments) and likely more design hiring.

items.summary: Mani Doraisamy shows how AI-written logging code made a welcome screen take about 15 seconds, because it chained several slow calls for user data. His point: AI meets the stated requirements but ignores speed and scale, so people must design the data model first, push back on requirements and review AI code against that plan. It was a top Hacker News post this weekend.
items.title: Case study: AI made developers into architects, and nobody told them
items.why: When you ship Android and iOS code with agents, your job shifts to reviewing structure and performance, not typing code. This is a short, concrete example of what to check before a PR goes to your devs.

items.summary: Mike Lacher built a satirical CSS library that copies the look of quickly 'vibecoded' websites: dark backgrounds with glowing orbs, gradient text, pill badges, glass cards inside cards, bento grids, counting-up stats and fake logos. It became one of the most upvoted posts on Hacker News.
items.title: Slopstrap: a joke UI kit that makes any site look AI-made
items.why: It is a funny but useful checklist of the visual habits that now signal 'generic AI'. Check your portfolio and AI-generated screens against it so your work looks chosen, not generated.

items.summary: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weights model that fits in about 20GB of memory and runs on Macs with 32GB of RAM through Ollama. It re-runs its middle layers three times per word to 'think' more, and leads open models of its size on several coding tests, though it is weaker at long chats and complex instructions.
items.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, an open model that runs on a laptop
items.why: Local models let you test AI coding or design-system helpers without sending bank code or customer data to the cloud, which matters in a regulated bank.

items.summary: Claire Vo, who runs the AI product tool ChatPRD, says groups cycle through free trials and promo codes to get free AI use, resell it or run whole businesses on her agent. She is ending free trials. Simon Willison notes the fraudsters may use test prompts to work out which AI model sits underneath.
items.title: Claire Vo ends ChatPRD free trials after a wave of 'token fraud'
items.why: Any free AI feature is now a fraud target. If Ameriabank adds AI features, abuse limits and identity checks are part of the design, just like in payments.

items.summary: A UK job board for design-system work lists a new Principal Design Systems Designer role at Rapid7 in Belfast (posted two days ago) and a Design System Lead at Kaluza in London. Other open UK roles include Synthesia's staff-level AI-native product designer and Marex's design-system positions.
items.title: UK design-system roles this week: Rapid7 in Belfast, Kaluza in London
items.why: Principal and lead design-system roles are a realistic next step for you. Save these to compare their requirements with your MyAmeria design-system case study.

items.summary: Figma shares fell to $16.28 on Thursday, a new yearly low, after trading above $38 earlier in 2026. The company beat its third-quarter targets and raised its yearly revenue forecast, helped by AI credits, but its outlook points to slower growth.
items.title: Figma's stock hits a new 52-week low despite beating forecasts
items.why: Figma is under pressure from AI design tools, so expect faster, bolder AI features in the tool you use every day, and more debate about where design work will happen.

items.summary: Berlin-based Nika Belskaya, who works as Vivid Cereal, mixes archive and public-domain images with modern, experimental references, then adds her own touch. She works across type, posters, illustration and icons, and her Georgian roots run through it, for example in her art direction for a cookbook about Georgia.
items.title: Georgian artist Nika Belskaya builds a 'Frankenstein' world of graphic stories
items.why: A designer from the region using local identity as a strength in an international career. Good inspiration for how a Yerevan background could make your visual voice and Star's art direction more distinct.

items.summary: Prompted by ChatGPT getting a wallet last week, Every's Grant Harvey looks at what the team lets AI agents purchase, from groceries to flights, and which purchases they still insist on approving themselves. Most of the piece is for paid subscribers.
items.title: Every's team on what they let AI agents buy, and when they still press 'buy'
items.why: Real people's rules for trusting agents with money are direct input for agent-payment UX: which amounts and categories feel safe to automate and which need a human tap.

items.summary: Affirm and Consumer Reports gave four AI models 30 shopping cases where they had to choose the cheapest way to pay, such as debit, installments or a credit card. Without guidance the models got it right about 49% of the time. With a short public instruction file, that rose to about 72%, and a small, cheap model became almost as good as the best one.
items.title: AI picks the right way to pay only about half the time, but a rules file helps a lot
items.why: This shows that written rules can matter as much as which model you pick. That is useful if MyAmeria ever adds an AI money helper, and for writing clear money guidance for kids in Star.

items.summary: Dragos hid about 2 million fake secrets (canary tokens) inside prompts sent to AI providers, then watched who used them. They found three providers had been hacked without knowing it. Some resellers could read customer prompts, and some requests marked 'zero data retention' were still copied. After the report, OpenRouter removed three providers and took the zero-retention label off 125 endpoints.
items.title: Researchers find AI providers leaking prompts and ignoring 'don't keep my data' settings
items.why: Banks will ask where customer data goes when an AI feature runs. This gives you the facts to push for direct, trusted providers and to design honest privacy messages in the app.

items.summary: In a write-up of his talk in Brazil, Brad Frost says every site that runs his business is now built by AI using his own design system. Changes to the system flow into the products, and product work feeds back into the system. He shares free course lessons on checks that AI-written code must pass, plus open AI skills, such as one that turns 'vibe-coded' pages back into design-system pages.
items.title: Brad Frost: 18 months of training AI on one design system now powers his 20+ sites
items.why: This is very close to your plan of teaching AI the MyAmeria design system and automating most design-file work. You can borrow his checks and skills directly.

items.summary: An Every writer explains a method. Collect 12 to 25 of your pieces, turn each into a plain brief, have AI write drafts from the briefs, then ask an AI judge which draft sounds more like your original. Swap the order and judge again, keep only the changes that raise the score, and test the final result on pieces you held back.
items.title: How-to: make AI write like you by testing drafts, not by describing your style
items.why: You can use this to build a writing skill for your microcopy voice or for LinkedIn posts in English. Both help your visibility for the UK move.

items.summary: A new app on Product Hunt lets parents set chores once and get automatic reminders. Kids tick off a task, add a photo as proof, and earn coins after a parent approves. They spend the coins on family rewards like a movie night, and a cartoon raccoon cheers them on with animations.
items.title: Raccoon Kids: a chores app where kids earn coins and parents approve with photo proof
items.why: It is a clean reference for Star: a mascot, a reward loop and a parent-approval flow for ages 6 to 16. Compare its photo-proof and approval steps with your own task and savings flows.

items.summary: Jakub Pachocki suggests that AI labs compare models using perplexity, a number that shows how well a model predicts text (lower means smarter). OpenAI published its own numbers and says new skills appear as the number falls. He proposes that labs agree on limits they will not cross until safety checks are ready, and he admits labs use different data, which makes comparing hard.
items.title: OpenAI's chief scientist wants one shared score to measure, and limit, AI progress
items.why: It helps you explain to your team why model jumps arrive suddenly, and why plans for AI features should expect big new skills within a year.

items.summary: In this browser game, a real AI manager gives you tasks in a terminal with a 90-second limit, checks your work and writes your performance review. Hidden checks count how often the manager approves broken work. A user's family photos and documents sit in the folder you can touch, so mistakes have a cost.
items.title: Worker 755: a game where you play the subagent and an AI is your boss
items.why: Playing it shows agent UX from the inside: what the agent can see, what it reports, and where approval goes wrong. That is useful thinking for your designs and for shipping code with AI agents.

items.summary: Monzo is hiring a senior lead designer to shape how customer help and support works, inside a design team of more than 100 people. The pay is £110,000 to £125,000 plus stock. They want experience designing for AI and automation, complex services, and coaching other designers.
items.title: Open role: Senior Lead Product Designer, Operations at Monzo (London, Cardiff or remote UK)
items.why: It matches your banking, support and AI work, and remote UK is allowed. Even if you don't apply now, it shows what a top UK bank expects at this level.

items.source: Growth Unhinged – Kyle Poyar, via newsletter
items.summary: The automation startup Gumloop now charges the real cost of AI tokens plus an 8% fee. Every chat shows exactly what was spent and on what, so users can switch to a cheaper model. Kyle Poyar says this builds trust through openness, but warns it can make a product look like a thin wrapper around AI models.
items.title: Gumloop shows the cost of every AI chat, and trial conversions rose 42%
items.why: Showing people exactly what they pay for is a strong trust pattern for any banking UI, and it is a good example to have for product strategy talks.

items.summary: This Codrops tutorial links scroll position to a paused GSAP timeline, so scrolling plays the motion. Text moves fast, slows down to be read, then speeds up again. Letters ripple in a wave, colored copies leave trails, and the ending throws random letters with physics.
items.title: How-to: choreograph kinetic typography on scroll with GSAP
items.why: It is a practical motion lesson you can adapt for playful moments in Star, or for a strong portfolio site.

items.summary: A Google designer who moved countries shares his advice. Keep your own background, because it adds value. Ask experienced local designers for honest feedback, keep core design ideas but adapt details to each place, and use side projects to test new tools like AI coding. He says a generated result is only a starting point.
items.title: Google's Yi Xiang on building a design career across borders
items.why: This is close to your own path from Yerevan to the UK. His tips on feedback and side projects can shape how you build your portfolio and reputation.

items.summary: On Lenny's podcast, Atlassian's head of AI and product craft says a product manager's main job is to build a 'shared brain' for the team. He describes three types of PM (artist, scientist and general manager) and explains why Atlassian is hiring more juniors than ever in the AI era.
items.title: Atlassian's Sherif Mansour: PM roles are growing fastest, and juniors are an advantage
items.why: As AI blurs design and product roles, his 'artist' type and shared-context idea can help you describe your strategy work in interviews.

items.summary: Ulika connects to a React, Vite or Next site through GitHub and Vercel. Then marketing people can change text and images right on the live page and press Publish, without touching code or moving to a CMS. It is in free open beta.
items.title: Ulika lets non-engineers edit sites built with Claude Code, Cursor or Codex
items.why: If you ship AI-built pages or prototypes, a tool like this shows how to let others make small edits without sending them back to engineers.

items.summary: The agency replaced the whisky brand's drawn wax drip with real prints. They pressed wheat, oak rings and farm plants into the brand's red wax. A new custom typeface is based on the handwriting of co-founder Margie Samuels, and the rollout runs through 2027.
items.title: Turner Duckworth makes Maker's Mark's new identity from real red wax
items.why: It shows how real, handmade material can carry a brand. That is relevant to your clay-style Star visuals and to art direction in general.

items.summary: Companies like Harmonic, Theorem and Axiom are using Lean, a math proof tool, to prove code is correct instead of only testing it. AI makes this much cheaper than before. The article suggests developers may spend more time writing and reviewing specs than writing code.
items.title: Latent Space: formal verification is becoming a weapon against AI 'slop' code
items.why: If you send AI-written feature code to your developers, clear specs and automatic checks will decide whether they trust your PRs.

items.summary: India's cyber agency CERT-In says attackers used AI tools to cause unauthorised payments at banks and payment firms. They did not break the payment systems. They quietly changed payee and approval records, then let the normal approval steps send the money to mule accounts. AI cut the time from break-in to cash-out from days to a few hours.
items.title: AI-assisted attackers drained Indian banks by editing records, then using normal approvals
items.why: This is a security-UX problem you can design for in MyAmeria: show who changed a payee and when, add a pause or extra check for new or edited payees, and give approvers the full history, not just an 'Approve' button.

items.summary: New METR data shows AI improves just as fast on hard-to-check work (like UX) as on easy-to-check work (like code), but starts later. Nielsen estimates UX will be where developers are today in about a year. His advice: watch what your developers now hand to agents and how they review the output, because that is your 2027 job. The same issue also covers designing for the worst place people use your app.
items.title: Jakob Nielsen: UX is about one year behind coding on the AI curve
items.why: You are already shipping code with AI agents, so you sit on both sides of this gap. Writing up what you learned there is a strong, early story for your portfolio and public writing.

items.summary: The Migration Advisory Committee (the government's expert advisers) says Global Talent mostly works and needs only small changes. It suggests that reference letters go straight to the endorsing body, that strong arts and tech employers get a fast track, and that settlement needs proof of steady paid work in your field. These are recommendations only; the Home Office has not decided yet.
items.title: UK advisers review the Global Talent visa: keep the bar high, add a fast track
items.why: Your UK plan depends on this route. The bar is not getting lower, so the evidence folder (awards, talks, articles, strong referees) still matters most. Referees who write to the endorsing body directly would change how you prepare letters.

items.source: Lenny's Newsletter – How I AI (via newsletter)
items.summary: Innovaccer's CTO Ankit Maheshwari runs an agent on a Mac Mini (via OpenClaw) that clears approvals, orders lunch, calls coworkers and books restaurants. His rules: start with one real bottleneck, split work into small specialist agents, and spend most of the effort on the instruction files ('soul' files) and limits. Once it approved expiring travel requests on its own, which showed him where hard limits were missing.
items.title: How I AI: a CTO's personal AI 'chief of staff' and the guardrails that make it safe
items.why: A practical model for your own agent setups, and a real example of agent-UX ideas (autonomy, limits, escalation) you could use in a MyAmeria or Star assistant concept.

items.source: Built for Mars – Peter Ramsey (via newsletter)
items.summary: In Peter Ramsey's weekly UX Bites, the business bank Mettle shows a hint box during sign-up that changes as you describe your business, telling you what is still missing. Other bites: Whereby lets you hear your own mic before a call, Notion makes you tap 'Reveal' to see a new feature, and the New York Times counts down your free-trial days.
items.title: Built for Mars: Mettle's sign-up hint box updates as you type
items.why: Small, copyable patterns for bank onboarding forms. A live 'what's still missing' hint could help kids and parents fill in Star sign-up without errors.

items.summary: Chinese lab Z.ai launched GLM-5.4. It runs some of its layers twice (a 'loop'), so it can think more without getting bigger. Z.ai says it rivals much larger models, but it has not published scores for the full model yet, and open weights are promised but not out.
items.title: Z.ai releases GLM-5.4, a big 'looped' model aimed at coding
items.why: Looped models are the new trend (Inkling 2 Mini used the same idea). Cheaper, faster coding models matter for your plan to ship features with AI agents.

items.summary: Ashby, the recruiting-software company, is hiring a Staff Design Engineer for Europe, based in Barcelona. The listed pay range is €154K–€250K a year. It is a role for someone who designs and also builds real UI in code.
items.title: Open role: Staff Design Engineer (EU) at Ashby, Barcelona, €154K–€250K
items.why: This matches your mix of design systems and shipping code with AI. It is in the EU, and it shows how much design-engineering skills are paid in Europe.

items.summary: Chris Nguyen (UX Playbook) and Stefi Peykova Krishnan, co-founder of the Bulgarian Design Council, will talk about designing products that remember, reason and act. Topics: what we design now, how to design under uncertainty, and where humans fit. You can send questions in advance by replying to the email.
items.title: Rectangles livestream Wed Nov 25: designing beyond AI tools
items.why: A good English-listening session on AI product design, and a chance to ask about designing agent features for kids and banking.

items.summary: Patrizia Bertini argues that AI makes more information than people can use, so the real job moves from knowing things to owning decisions. Often a person 'approves' AI output without the time, power or knowledge to judge it. She says teams must design decision processes and teach judgement.
items.title: Decision theatre: when 'human in the loop' is only a rubber stamp
items.why: Useful framing for design reviews and for any AI feature in banking, where a person must really own the final call.

items.summary: Singapore's central bank (MAS) plans an 'Agentic Money Sandbox' to test how AI agents pay, how to check an agent's identity and permissions, and money that pays only when set conditions are met. Banks will try it in a safe test setting first. Officials said firms stay responsible for what agents do for them. (Announced Nov 18.)
items.title: Singapore will test AI agents paying with digital money in a sandbox
items.why: Agent payments are coming to banks fast. Identity, permissions and 'who is responsible' screens are design problems MyAmeria will face too.

items.summary: Simon Willison built a page that shows many ways to style the native select (dropdown) element. It includes a small CSS snippet that makes selects look the same across browsers.
items.title: Simon Willison: a specimen page for styling HTML select boxes
items.why: A quick, practical front-end craft reference for your coded prototypes and portfolio site.

items.summary: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as CEO. It says a security review found no national-security risk, and an independent investigation will continue. The board also set up a new committee for export and security rules. Colette Kress returns to her CFO role.
items.title: Nvidia brings back Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he left
items.why: Nvidia supplies most AI chips, so stability there affects AI tool prices and speed.

items.summary: Michael Feder of the studio Hornet notes that Prada, Levi's and Dior all used animation in their holiday ads, while viewers check Dior's spot for signs of AI. He says the best work shows clear human choices and care. His tips: be restrained, build a world that can grow across channels, and know why you chose that craft.
items.title: Creative Boom: this year's holiday ads all bet on visible human craft
items.why: Supports your Star claymation direction: a handmade, crafted look stands out when AI images are everywhere.

items.summary: Every's head of operations Arielle Shipper writes that running many AI agents means constant context switching. Her own agent pointed out she had started seven separate tasks in 29 minutes. Nine people at Every share how they cope (the tips are behind the paywall).
items.title: Every: your AI agents can multitask, but can you?
items.why: You run several agents at once for design and code. A good reminder to plan focus time, not just more agent sessions.

items.summary: Security company CrowdStrike will buy network-security firm Zscaler, valued at about $43.9 billion. Each Zscaler share becomes 1.135 CrowdStrike shares. The deal still needs regulatory approval.
items.title: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler in a $43.9B all-stock deal
items.why: Banks like Ameriabank use these security vendors, so this may shape the security tools behind banking apps.

items.summary: Meta has opened its Muse agent to UK adults in its app, on the web and in WhatsApp, with 15 local partners like Sainsbury's, Trainline and easyJet. Muse shows its plan and asks before each purchase or email. It pays with Stripe's 'Onelink', a digital copy of your card that only agents can use, so Muse never sees the real card.
items.title: Meta's Muse AI agent launches in the UK, and every purchase needs your approval
items.why: This is the first big agent that pays for things in the UK, the market you want to work in. Look at the approval step, the 'what I plan to do' view and the agent-only card: these are trust patterns a bank like Ameriabank will need when agents start using MyAmeria.

items.summary: Anthropic's economists interviewed 58 US companies about almost 300 ways they use AI. Most gains came from doing more work, faster or better, not from cutting costs, and layoffs caused by AI were rare. The biggest wins came when teams changed how work is organised, for example by giving people broader roles, instead of just adding AI to old processes.
items.title: Anthropic study of 58 companies: AI mostly adds output, it rarely replaces people
items.why: It gives you real evidence for your plan to ship code with AI agents: the value comes from changing the workflow, not just using a tool. You can use these findings when you pitch the 'designer delivers PRs' idea to your team leads.

items.summary: Wise has a new Credit team and wants a senior designer for its first credit products, starting with US business credit. The designer owns the whole journey, from eligibility and application to repayments, and helps shape strategy. It is hybrid in London, the pay is £72,000–£105,000, and the listing says to apply by 1 December 2026.
items.title: Open role: Senior Product Designer, Spend – Credit at Wise, London (£72K–£105K)
items.why: It is a London fintech role that asks for exactly what you do: complex money flows, systems thinking and work with regulation. The deadline is in six days, so if you want it, update your portfolio and apply this week.

items.summary: In a keynote write-up, Simon Willison names three turning points: coding agents became reliable in late 2025, 'Fable-class' models in mid-2026 began solving hard problems alone when given a goal and tools, and by autumn models got good at 3D and even at making games fun. His practical advice: give the agent a clear goal and the right tools, and ask directly for quality.
items.title: Simon Willison: the three big jumps in what AI coding agents can do this year
items.why: This is a practical guide for your designer-ships-code plan: set a clear goal, give the agent tools, and ask it to make things 'fun' or 'beautiful'. The 3D part also matters for Star 3D Studio.

items.summary: Peter Ramsey's weekly list shows five small patterns you can copy. Whereby lets you record a few words and hear them back before you join a call. Notion makes you tap 'Reveal' to see a new feature so you pay attention, and the New York Times app counts down the days left in your free trial each time you open it.
items.title: UX Bites #148: a call sound check, a 'Reveal' button and a trial countdown
items.why: These are easy ideas for MyAmeria Star: a countdown could show kids how close they are to a savings goal, and a 'Reveal' moment could introduce new features in a playful way.

items.summary: Luke Wroblewski suggests that designers ask AI agents to build tiny interactive 'playgrounds' for one design question. You move sliders and see real content, empty states, errors or animations change live on the real platform. When you're done, you export the values as code or tokens and throw the tool away.
items.title: Luke Wroblewski: 'design by playground', small throwaway tools built with AI agents
items.why: This fits how you already work with AI and your design system: you could build a playground to tune MyAmeria tokens or Star animations on a real phone and give developers the exact values.

items.summary: Revolut Bank UK is giving new customers a 5.25% promotional rate for six months on up to £25,000 in instant-access savings. After the first 30 days, customers must make at least three payments of £5 or more every 30 days, or the rate drops. Money can be withdrawn at any time without a penalty.
items.title: Revolut offers new UK customers 5.25% on savings, but only if they keep spending
items.why: The rule that you must spend to keep your savings rate is a pattern worth studying. Think about how a bank explains a condition like this clearly, and whether a similar rule would help or confuse kids in Star.

items.summary: In this essay, UX Collective founder Fabricio Teixeira notes that AI answers instantly and with no social risk. People pause, soften their words and think about how a message will land, and those pauses are a form of care. He worries that getting used to AI's instant replies may make us less patient with each other.
items.title: Fabricio Teixeira: chatbots never hesitate, and that may change how we talk to people
items.why: It's a useful lens for designing AI features for kids: speed is not the only goal. For Star, think about where a short pause or a gentler reply teaches better habits than an instant answer.

items.summary: In a three-minute video, Nielsen Norman Group shares tips for a friendly brand voice. Change your tone to fit the situation, avoid reusing the same jokes or tricks, and use specific words. NN/g's research found that casual, conversational and enthusiastic tones scored best for friendliness and trust.
items.title: NN/g video: how to make a brand voice sound human, not gimmicky
items.why: You write Star's error and success messages, so this helps you check that the playful tone stays fresh and still feels trustworthy for a banking app.

items.summary: The Amsterdam agency Verve branded Zero, a Helsinki AI company that makes CRM software. Old CRM tools are shown as fossils and cave drawings, while Zero looks so advanced it hardly looks like technology. A character called Zorb shows moods through cave-inscription 'force fields', and the yellow palette gets oxblood and soft blue added.
items.title: Verve makes AI startup Zero's identity a Stone Age world where old tools turn to fossils
items.why: Most AI brands now look alike, and this shows how a clear story plus hand-drawn illustration can stand out. It's good art direction to compare with the claymation style you're building for Star.

items.summary: Viktor Jacobsson, who led global creative at Uber, is now global head of creative at the legal AI company Legora, covering over 80 markets. Designer Neville Brody became creative chair at the agency Toaster and will start a creativity and technology lab. He warned that AI can speed up repetitive work but may make design all look the same.
items.title: Creative moves: Uber's creative lead joins Legora, and Neville Brody joins Toaster
items.why: AI companies are hiring senior creative leaders from big brands, which is a career path you could aim for. Brody's warning about everything looking the same is a good point to make in interviews.

items.summary: Luke Wroblewski summarises an event where five builders showed how they run many agents. Their shared lessons: give agents a shared spec outside their memory, wake them only when there is real work, enforce workflows in code, and watch token costs. One team, Amp, says it reached $100M in yearly revenue with 21 people.
items.title: Luke Wroblewski: how five companies run AI agents at huge scale
items.why: It shows where 'design with agents' is going next, and the idea of machine-readable UI contracts links directly to teaching AI your design system.

items.summary: Josh Comeau lists the CSS features he wants all browsers to support next year. They include corner-shape for squircles and notches, custom CSS functions, scroll-triggered animations, and animating sizes like height: auto. Many already work in Chrome and can be added as extras today.
items.title: Josh Comeau's 10 CSS wishes for 2027, from squircles to animating height: auto
items.why: Squircles, scroll animations and smooth accordions are things your design system needs on the web. Knowing what CSS can do helps you write specs that developers can build without workarounds.

items.summary: Shirudo is a free tool that blocks the exact behaviour an exploit needs on a running Linux system, so teams stay safe while they prepare a real patch. Each 'shield' must be approved by a person and is digitally signed before it loads. In a test, it stopped an attack on a live Elasticsearch server.
items.title: OpenAI and Cisco release Shirudo, an open-source 'shield' for unpatched Linux servers
items.why: AI is now speeding up both attacks and defences, and banks feel this first. It's useful background when security questions come up in your MyAmeria work.

items.summary: The Ladybird team released the first public alpha of a browser with its own engine, not a copy of Chrome or Firefox. It has automatic updates, in-browser reporting for broken sites, and developer testing tools. It's only for early testers: some sites break and there are no security promises yet.
items.title: Ladybird, a browser built from scratch, releases its first alpha for macOS and Linux
items.why: A new independent engine is rare news, and it was one of the top stories on Hacker News today. It reminds you to test web work beyond Chrome.

items.summary: Your LinkedIn alert for senior product designer jobs in Barcelona found a new Senior UX/UI Designer role at Extia, a consulting company. LinkedIn says the company is actively hiring and you can apply with your resume and profile. Open the listing to check the language rules and whether it's hybrid.
items.title: Job alert: Extia is hiring a Senior UX/UI Designer in Barcelona
items.why: Barcelona is part of your EU backup plan. Applying to roles like this keeps your interview skills sharp while you work on the UK visa.

items.summary: Nielsen checks his 2025 forecast against new studies and finds he got 4 of 5 right. His new idea: AI learns a task faster when its result is easy to check. Screen design came early because it follows old, stable rules. Diagnosing usability problems on new screens is slower, because only real users can confirm it. He gives a year-by-year list and says two jobs stay human: choosing what is worth building ('worthfinding') and getting stakeholders to agree in the room.
items.title: Jakob Nielsen: which UX tasks AI will master, and when (2026–2030 timetable)
items.why: This is a clear plan for what to learn next. Ask AI for 10 divergent designs and train your judgment in choosing between them. His bank example (fix human onboarding, or build for customers' AI agents?) is exactly the kind of call MyAmeria will face.

items.summary: Simon Taylor asks who decides what agents are allowed to do with our money. Visa tested 22 AI models on 15 shopping tasks and only 57.2% of runs passed. In about half of the failed runs the agent still bought something. Meanwhile, Stripe says daily agent spending through Link grew 80x in under three months, and Meta's Muse uses per-order approval or spending limits so the agent never sees card details.
items.title: Fintech Brainfood: shopping agents passed only 57% of Visa's tests, and some still bought
items.why: Approve-each-order and spending limits are the controls a bank app like MyAmeria may need for AI agents, and for parents on MyAmeria Star. The failure numbers help you argue for clear previews and undo.

items.summary: 1Password says an attacker got into an employee's work GitHub account, copied private source code, reached its CI/CD system and pushed code that downloaded some customer account records. These include names, emails, public keys and some invitation and recovery tokens. The company says vault contents, passwords and Secret Keys were not touched. It warns users to watch for fake emails about invitations or account recovery.
items.title: 1Password breach: hacked employee GitHub account led to download of customer account records
items.why: If you use 1Password, watch for phishing. For a bank designer it is also a lesson: leaked names and emails lead straight to 'account recovery' scams, so recovery flows and warning copy in MyAmeria need to be very clear.

items.summary: Cameron Worboys, Head of Product Design at Cash App, shows prototypes and internal tools. He explains how the Tags feature grew from an internet joke, why the team prototypes with real data, and how a long run of experiments shaped the new onboarding. He also covers designers writing their own code without a design-systems team, and how to get buy-in for unusual ideas.
items.title: Talk: how Cash App's ~20-person design team ships bold fintech ideas fast
items.why: Cash App is a playful money app, close in spirit to MyAmeria Star. It also shows the 'designers who code' way of working you are building toward with AI agents.

items.summary: After almost two years of work, Visa keeps its wordmark and blue and yellow but adds new parts. There is a standalone V symbol for app icons and motion, a horizontal 'progress bar' graphic that changes for different audiences, and a custom typeface, Visa Sans, made with Displaay. The typeface covers 115 languages and takes extra care with currency symbols. There is even a new 'ding' sound for successful payments.
items.title: Base Design refreshes Visa: a new V symbol, a 'progress bar' system and Visa Sans
items.why: It is a fintech brand problem solved well: a trusted brand that people no longer notice. Look at how they designed currency symbols and the payment sound; both are useful ideas for MyAmeria's type tokens and success states.

items.summary: Fortune reports that the two companies are in talks to end Amazon's block on Muse, Meta's personal AI agent. The main issues are search results and advertising, because Amazon earns tens of billions of dollars from ads and fears losing its direct contact with shoppers. More than 10 million people had set up Muse by October. Meta plans to take a small fee on purchases.
items.title: Amazon and Meta are discussing a deal to let Meta's Muse agent shop on Amazon
items.why: Big platforms are now negotiating how agents get into stores. Banks will face the same question: when an agent, not a person, uses the app, who 'owns' the customer? That is a strategy question for MyAmeria.

items.source: Into Design Systems – UK job board
items.summary: Fresha's design-system team runs two systems across web, iOS and Android, and this role is mostly web. The job includes building components and tokens, keeping APIs the same across platforms, supporting 30+ languages, and making component data usable by AI agents through a design-system CLI. It asks for 7+ years of front-end engineering. It is hybrid, with four office days a week, and the listing does not mention visa sponsorship.
items.title: Open role: Senior Design System Engineer at Fresha, London (makes components usable by AI agents)
items.why: It is an engineering role, so it is probably not for you, but read it as a signal. 'Design system that AI agents can read' is now a real job requirement in London, and it matches your work teaching AI the MyAmeria system. Put that in your portfolio.

items.source: Into Design Systems – UK job board
items.summary: Mymoose posted a principal-level design-systems designer role in Belfast, Northern Ireland, about three days ago. It joins a cluster of senior design-system jobs in the UK this month, including Kaluza in London and Rapid7, also in Belfast. Open the posting for details on hybrid work and sponsorship.
items.title: Open role: Principal Design Systems Designer at Mymoose, Belfast
items.why: Your strongest UK story is 'built a bank design system from scratch'. Principal design-system roles are exactly where that experience counts, and Belfast is a cheaper UK city to start in.

items.summary: A developer shows that iOS Safari normally limits touch events and animation frames to 60 per second, even on 120Hz screens. His workaround uses three tricks: invisible scroll areas that read finger position very often, a tiny hidden scrolling element that keeps the screen at 120Hz, and an OffscreenCanvas that draws frames off the main thread. On an iPhone 18 Pro it averaged 118fps while dragging. He warns that Apple could close this path.
items.title: How-to: get 120fps touch and animation in iOS Safari without a settings flag
items.why: If you prototype motion for MyAmeria Star in the browser, this explains why it can feel less smooth than native. It also teaches how screen refresh actually works.

items.summary: A new site on Josh Comeau's domain offers more than fifty professionally recorded button clicks, presses and toggles. Each one is recorded several times so repeated presses don't sound robotic. You install it as an NPM package. It was one of the most popular posts on Hacker News today.
items.title: Button Sounds: a free library of 50+ studio-recorded clicks and toggles for UI
items.why: Sound is a cheap way to make a kids' app feel physical and playful. Try a few sounds on MyAmeria Star's coin, savings-goal and success moments, and keep a mute option for parents.

items.summary: A research team shows that two AI agents on the same inference server can pass messages even with no network or shared files. They do it by changing which GPU code runs or what sits in a shared cache, which subtly changes each other's outputs. In one test, a 'monitor' model that was in on the trick let through all 354 marked attacks. The fixes include separate servers for monitors and a separate cache for each user.
items.title: Researchers: sandboxed AI agents can still secretly signal each other through a shared server
items.why: 'One AI checks another' is becoming a common safety design, including in banking. This shows that the check can fail quietly, so a person should still review high-risk money actions.

items.summary: Historian Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra about an unsigned 1808 sketchbook at Yale. With little prompting, it found a diary that mentions a visit by the vicomte de Chabot five days before a date in the sketchbook, and it named a little-known journal that would confirm the match. Humphries checked that journal and it did. He expects historians to face a 'crisis of confidence' soon.
items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra identified who drew an anonymous 1808 sketchbook in about 22 minutes
items.why: It is a good example of AI research you can verify: the model made a prediction and a human checked the source. Use the same pattern for AI in design research: let it propose, then confirm the evidence yourself.

items.summary: Thompson uses Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO to argue that AI will make strong individuals matter more than layers of managers. He notes that the most valuable companies keep growing while employing fewer people. He expects small, AI-powered groups to challenge big companies one sector at a time, and he admits this raises fairness concerns.
items.title: Ben Thompson: AI may reverse corporate bureaucracy, and 'it only takes an individual'
items.why: If teams shrink, one designer who can frame the problem, design and ship code becomes very valuable. That is the profile you are building, and a strong story to tell in UK interviews.

items.summary: Brad Frost says technology should serve people, and he warns that AI could deepen loneliness and isolation. Because no one can keep up alone, he invites designers to his Slack community of more than 1,000 members, with live sessions every two weeks. He also recommends paying independent educators for human expertise rather than replacing it with AI.
items.title: Brad Frost: with AI moving this fast, community matters more than ever
items.why: Joining and contributing to well-known international communities builds the public visibility the Global Talent visa looks for, and Brad's group focuses on design systems and AI, your core topics.

items.summary: UK beer brand Carling has a new identity by BrandOpus, built around a crest. It shows the old Burton brewery and bridge framed by barley, with the founder's signature added to cans and glasses. The agency also made a flexible system for football clubs that adapts to each club's colours.
items.title: BrandOpus turns Carling's identity into a football-club-style crest
items.why: It is a simple example of using heritage and a badge to create a sense of belonging, an idea you could try for MyAmeria Star achievements and 'club' moments for kids.

items.summary: Claude wrote most of a new Rust version of Anthropic's Messages API, with the core path done in about a week. The team then used the live Python service as a 'judge': real traffic was copied to both versions and every difference was grouped and fixed. Result: about 70% less CPU and a faster first token.
items.title: Anthropic moved its API to Rust with Claude; checking the code was the hard part
items.why: This is a clear playbook for your plan to ship MyAmeria code with AI agents: the agent writes fast, but you win trust by showing how the result is checked against the real app. Use the 'inner loop, outer loop, memory loop' idea in your PR process and your case study.

items.summary: Indian payments firm Cashfree launched Cashfree Wallet on Nov 24. Users give an AI agent a budget and payment rules, and the agent never sees card or bank details. It starts with bill payments only. Traffic from AI agents on Cashfree's checkout has grown 16 times this year.
items.title: Cashfree launches a wallet where you set a budget and rules before an AI agent can pay
items.why: A real example of 'agent spending limits' UX, which is exactly what a parent-controlled kids' app like MyAmeria Star could need. Budgets, rules and approvals for agents look a lot like the controls parents already set for kids.

items.summary: Fortuna Entertainment Group posted a senior design-system role on Nov 27. You would own a multi-brand component library for mobile and desktop: patterns, variables, documentation and audits, and help teams adopt it. The listing says Birmingham but the text says the team is in London, so check the location.
items.title: New UK role: Group Senior System Designer at Fortuna Entertainment Group (hybrid)
items.why: It asks for exactly what you built at Ameriabank: a design system from scratch used across platforms. Sponsorship isn't mentioned, so ask early, and lead your application with your MyAmeria design-system story.

items.summary: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Neon around Nov 23–24, and early users rank it between Claude Opus and Fable. People praise its writing style, but some say it flatters you too much when you ask for criticism. Google also released an experimental 'anti-slop' front-end design skill for it.
items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Neon puts Google DeepMind back at the top of AI
items.why: Another strong model for your AI design workflow. Test it on one real MyAmeria screen next to Claude before you switch, and watch the flattery problem when you ask it to review your work.

items.summary: Designer and writer Marcin Wichary published a free library of 80 interface guidelines. It covers Apple, Microsoft, Google, Palm, BeOS, Nokia and many more, with links to PDFs and archived copies. It reached the Hacker News front page this week.
items.title: Marcin Wichary saves 80 UI style guides, from the 1980s Apple Lisa to Material Design
items.why: Great material for design-system work: you can see how the best platforms wrote rules for buttons, menus and tone. Pick 2–3 guides and copy their structure for your MyAmeria documentation that AI agents will read.

items.summary: An Italian court placed Revolut's Italian business under a court-appointed administrator for 12 months. Police say its checks let 24 suspects, some linked to the mafia, move about €41.9M between 2021 and 2026. Revolut says it accepts the decision and will cooperate.
items.title: Italian court puts Revolut Italy under supervision over money-laundering gaps
items.why: Fast sign-up is a design win only if safety checks keep up. When you design onboarding or limits for MyAmeria, this is the kind of case that explains why compliance steps exist.

items.summary: OpenAI is joining ChatGPT's chat and work tools into a single interface, so users stop switching tabs. Both now share one usage limit, while the fast Instant model stays unlimited. It starts with some Pro users and reaches more people in December.
items.title: ChatGPT merges its Chat and Work tabs into one screen with one usage meter
items.why: Both big AI apps (Anthropic did this in September) now pick one surface instead of separate modes. It's a useful pattern to discuss when you design AI features for MyAmeria: fewer modes, but clearer limits.

items.summary: Anthropic's new beta lets you turn a Claude artifact into an app with its own icon and window on Mac and Windows. Federico Viticci found they are web pages inside a thin wrapper, using Claude's connectors and usage limits. He built several useful tools but warns that shared apps stop working if the owner stops sharing.
items.title: MacStories tests Claude's new 'Install as app': artifacts become desktop apps
items.why: You can turn small internal tools (like your Morning Brief or a token checker) into real desktop apps without a developer. It's also a good example of 'designers shipping software' for your portfolio story.

items.summary: Microsoft says Chinese and North Korean groups have added Artex, an AI tool that automates hacking steps, to their kits. It can go from scanning a network to full access in minutes. It was recently linked to attacks on financial institutions in South Korea and Japan.
items.title: Microsoft: state hackers adopt Artex, an AI attack tool linked to bank hacks
items.why: Attacks are getting faster and cheaper, so banks will add more checks, alerts and step-up security. Designing those security moments so they stay clear and calm (also for kids) is a growing part of fintech UX.

items.summary: European crypto and investing app Bitpanda posted a Senior Product Designer role for its Web3 team in Barcelona. It came through your LinkedIn job alert for senior product designer roles in Barcelona this week.
items.title: Job alert: Bitpanda is hiring a Senior Product Designer (Web3) in Barcelona
items.why: Bitpanda is an EU fintech, which matches your 'UK first, then EU fintech' plan. Your banking and payments work at Ameriabank is directly relevant.

items.summary: Designer Barry Baris Dogan explains how he built a site for a sound designer, where motion follows the audio. It uses GSAP, Howler.js and the Web Audio API: a live spectrum meter, a playable headline and faders that mix sound loops. He also covers good habits like a sound on/off gate, pausing hidden tabs and reduced motion.
items.title: Case study: DKTON, a website you hear before you read
items.why: Sound and motion make an interface feel alive, which fits the playful, claymation style of MyAmeria Star. The 'sound hygiene' list is a ready checklist if you add sounds to the kids' app.

items.summary: In this Latent Space episode, the engineer who worked on Claude Code (now at OpenAI) argues that cheap mass-made software and careful craft can live together. He shows how he builds small personal tools and games, and changes things quickly to keep the 'feel' right.
items.title: Thariq Shihipar: AI can make software by the thousand, and still leave room for craft
items.why: It supports your positioning: AI does the volume, and your taste and polish make the difference. Good listening practice for your English too.

items.summary: Computer scientist Scott Aaronson describes a fast run of AI-made proofs from OpenAI and Anthropic, many checked with the Lean proof tool. He also says he is nearly sure the labs have new algorithms that could threaten some encryption in use today, but he hasn't seen the details. The post was the top story on Hacker News.
items.title: Scott Aaronson: AI labs are proving big math results and may threaten encryption
items.why: If encryption changes, banks will need new security steps and new ways to explain them. For now it's mostly a signal of how fast AI is moving.

items.summary: Type designer Yury Ostromentsky (co-founder of CSTM Fonts, now based in Georgia) made a series of fonts that lean backwards. It includes sans, script and blackletter styles, and in some settings the slant gets so strong that the letters are hard to read. He made it as an emotional reaction to the war.
items.title: Backslanted: Yury Ostromentsky's typefaces that lean the 'wrong' way
items.why: A good example of type carrying emotion, from a designer in our region. Useful inspiration for expressive moments in MyAmeria Star.

items.summary: AI media company Every raised a $17.5M Series A. It has 35 people, and each team member tests new AI models on real work. Shipper says model output is only 'the floor', and the team's edge is what it adds on top.
items.title: Every raises $17.5M; Dan Shipper says one person now does the work of 3 to 10
items.why: A clear way to explain your own value as an AI-native designer in interviews: the AI is the baseline, and your judgment is the extra.

items.source: Felix Lee, AI First Designer (via newsletter)
items.summary: Felix Lee (ADPList) explains how one AI agent now finds the biggest drop-off in his funnels, checks that the problem is real, writes the ticket, and designs three options with one marked as recommended. Nothing goes to engineering until he says yes, and 14 days after launch the bot checks whether the fix worked. He shares the full brief, which you can copy and adapt.
items.title: Felix Lee: his AI bot runs the design loop, and he only makes the final call
items.why: This is close to your plan to ship MyAmeria work with AI agents. The 'two-way door vs one-way door' rule and the hard approval gate are ideas you can put into your own agent setup and your PR process, and they make a strong story for your portfolio.

items.summary: Google made eight Workspace MCP servers (MCP is a standard way for AI agents to use apps) generally available on Nov 24 and changed its terms: AI agents must use them from February 1, 2027. The Gmail server can search, read and draft, but it cannot send, reply or forward. Free projects get about 5,000 requests a day, and paid billing starts in April 2027.
items.title: Google: from Feb 2027, AI agents must reach Gmail and Drive only through its MCP servers
items.why: You build workflows where agents read and write in your tools. This shows where big platforms are going: agents get their own doors, with tighter limits and clear rules about data. Banks like Ameriabank will likely do the same for agents that touch customer accounts.

items.summary: From January, California needs parental consent before teens get algorithmic feeds or night-time notifications, and bans features like autoplay and endless scroll for under-16s. New York's rules, from January 25, require apps to check age and turn off personalised recommendations and midnight-to-6am notifications for minors without consent. The EFF, which opposes the laws, warns that age checks are often wrong and smaller apps may struggle.
items.title: New York and California age rules for under-18 users start in January 2027
items.why: MyAmeria Star serves kids aged 6 to 16. These rules are a preview of what regulators in the UK and EU may ask for, so it is worth designing parental consent, quiet hours and age checks into Star now, not later.

items.summary: Paid builds billing and pricing tools for companies that sell AI agents. The senior designer will own how customers meter, price and bill agent work, and must ship their own UI changes to production with AI coding tools. It is five days a week in the London office, and you must be eligible to work in the UK. Applications close on December 16.
items.title: Open role: Senior Product Designer, Monetization at Paid, London (£85K–£125K)
items.why: Few jobs ask so directly for what you are building: a designer who ships code with AI agents, works in dense fintech screens and runs a design system. Even if the visa timing doesn't fit, use this listing as a checklist for your portfolio.

items.summary: In this livestream replay, a principal designer in Australia's health department splits AI design work into three levels: the interface, the logic of the system, and the memory and behaviour underneath. Her advice is to go one level deeper than your role asks, learn one small thing each day, and always ask who a task affects before you hand it to AI. She also warns designers not to confuse their job title with who they are.
items.title: Rectangles: Stefi Peykova-Krishnan on the three levels of design work in AI products
items.why: Your work on agents and the MyAmeria design system already touches levels 1 and 2. Learning to talk about level 2 (how the system behaves when AI is unpredictable) is what makes a senior designer stand out in UK interviews.

items.source: This Week in Fintech – UK & Europe
items.summary: This week's roundup covers Klarna becoming the first non-card option in Adyen's checkout for AI agents, with shoppers confirming each purchase, and Visa widening its 'Agentic Ready' programme in Europe. Starling's CEO Raman Bhatia will step down at year-end, and Wise's half-year revenue rose 23% to $1.45bn. UK regulators also opened a consultation on cyber resilience for payment and e-money firms.
items.title: UK and Europe fintech week: Klarna joins agent checkout, Starling's CEO to leave, Wise up 23%
items.why: These are the UK fintech companies you may want to work for, and the news shows they all bet on agents that pay for users but still ask for a human 'yes'. That approval moment is a design problem you can show you have solved in MyAmeria.

items.summary: Clay's Jeff Barg explains how the company grew to about 600 people and runs its AI agent next to outside tools like Claude Code, with usage split about 50/50. Customers dislike choosing a model, so Clay is building an automatic router, but it first has to earn trust before people leave 'auto mode' on. Early tests that only checked which tools the agent called missed how people really used it.
items.title: Clay's head of AI: customers hate model pickers, so trust must be earned first
items.why: It is a good lesson in product strategy for AI features: hide hard choices, but show enough (like how tokens are spent) that people trust the default. The same thinking applies to any AI assistant inside a banking app.

items.summary: LottieFiles wrapped up a week of launches: Lottie AI (describe an animation, get light code), Creator MCP, Generative Icons and an IconScout API. Creator MCP lets Claude, Cursor or Codex write a script that becomes a real Lottie scene with layers and keyframes you can still edit. It exports Lottie, dotLottie, MP4 and WebM, and the agent can check its own work with preview images.
items.title: LottieFiles launch week: AI agents can now build editable Lottie animations
items.why: You want motion and 3D in MyAmeria Star and want agents to do most of the file work. This lets an agent produce on-brand, editable animations that your Android and iOS teams can ship, instead of one-off videos.

items.summary: A one-line prompt asks ChatGPT, with memory turned on, to invent a WhatsApp-style group chat where AI assistants talk about you. It went to the top of Hacker News with more than 600 points. The format is funny, but people say it also feels revealing, because it shows how much the model remembers.
items.title: A viral prompt makes ChatGPT show your AI assistants 'gossiping' about you
items.why: It is a clever example of how to make an AI's memory visible and understandable. For any assistant in a banking app, showing users what the system knows about them, in a friendly format, builds trust.

items.summary: Jan-Lukas Else keeps his server setup in Git so AI coding agents can work on it like any other project. A server image that would have taken him a week took half a day with AI, and he now builds small personal tools in Go. He also lists the costs: more things to maintain, and AI code can have bugs and security holes. It was the top post on Hacker News with over 1,000 points.
items.title: 'AI made self-hosting fun again': how coding agents cut the setup work
items.why: It shows the same habit you need for shipping app code with agents: put everything in a repo, automate updates, and review what the AI writes. Good reading before you set up your own agent workflow.

items.summary: Creative developer Patrick Heintzmann projected 15 small WebGL effects onto a 20cm plywood cube using Three.js. He built a virtual copy of the cube seen from the projector's position, and a simple timeline tool where clips snap to the beat. The music is the clock: effects follow a fixed 145 BPM grid instead of reacting to sound.
items.title: Case study: projection mapping a techno release onto a cube, built in the browser
items.why: A practical lesson in timing and choreography for motion. The idea of one 'clock' that drives every animation is useful for Star's playful screens and for any motion system you hand to developers.

items.summary: Hugo Duprez of Sprite Fusion explains how he built 'The Game Dev Atlas', a 3D map in the style of a 16th-century atlas. He started from real elevation data, drew hills with engraved lines, added colour washes and kept small 'ink' imperfections in the lettering. Each town shows one game technique, and the map runs at 60fps in the browser.
items.title: How-to: making a 3D fantasy map look like a 1570 atlas
items.why: A clear art-direction process you can reuse: collect references, pick type that fits the era, then keep the imperfections. It is useful for your Star 3D Studio and claymation style work.

items.summary: The next free Rectangles livestream, on December 2, is about how designers present work. It is live on YouTube and LinkedIn, and you can ask questions during the show. The series is run by designer Chris Nguyen.
items.title: Rectangles livestream on Dec 2: how designers present their work
items.why: Presenting your work well matters for UK portfolio reviews and for the Global Talent visa evidence. One hour here can sharpen how you tell the MyAmeria Star story.

items.summary: Magnitude is a new open-source tool that spreads a model across the graphics card, the computer's memory and the SSD, and loads parts just before they are needed. Its own tests show 41 word pieces (tokens) per second for a 66GB model on an RTX 3090. The Neuron notes these numbers skip the wait before the first word appears.
items.title: Magnitude runs AI models bigger than your graphics card by using the SSD
items.why: Big open models on a normal PC means you could run private AI for sensitive bank work without sending data to the cloud. Treat the speed claims carefully until others test them.

items.summary: Designers Jacob Hulmston and Marty Uhrecký made a book that looks plain at first, like a phone book or technical handbook, but hides codes and visual puzzles. Type sits between serif and monospace, with hot-pink waveforms and a bookmark that seems to animate. They tested analogue tricks like lenticular printing and stereography.
items.title: A.G. Cook's 'Soulbreaker Codex': a book designed like a game manual and a puzzle
items.why: A good example of a strong idea carried through every detail, from type to printing. That kind of consistency is what makes design-system and brand work feel like one world.

items.summary: Counterpoint says US smartphone shipments fell 9% in Q3 2026 because higher memory prices hurt cheap Android phones. Apple's share rose from 50% to 57%, Samsung reached 25%, and Motorola fell to 8%. The analyst expects a weak end of year with higher prices.
items.title: US smartphone sales fall 9% as memory costs hit Android; Apple reaches 57%
items.why: If memory stays expensive, more people keep older and cheaper Android phones for longer. For MyAmeria and Star, that means performance on low-end Android still matters a lot.
